docs.title: KikoLens
docs.text: Private, local-first data analysis. Load a dataset, let the autopilot take a first pass, clean it, explore it, test hypotheses, compare many models and understand them, forecast, study customers and the effect of a change, watch a data source over time, and keep what you built: a recipe you can replay, a model you can score new data with, a panel and a report. Nothing leaves your machine; the optional language-model features use Ollama running locally.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
pip install "kikolens @ git+https://github.com/Francisco-B-O/kikolens.git"
kikolens doctor       # check the installation
kikolens start        # open the dashboard, then pick "Or try an example" or load your own file
If you want to... Read Click through the app Dashboard guide Script it or run it on a schedule Command line and pipelines Use it from a notebook Python API and Jupyter Follow a complete example Workflows Know how a result is computed and when not to trust it How it works Change settings (Ollama, port, language) Configuration Contribute Development

docs.title: What is in the box
docs.text:
• Data: home page, data story, chart gallery, quality and cleaning (undoable, as replayable recipes), privacy tools, record matching, transformations, an autopilot and an analyst that chats with your data.
  • Analysis: statistical tests with effect sizes, sequential and Bayesian A/B tests, anomalies, drift, segmentation, "why did it change", causal effect and survival.
  • Models: a model lab (cross-validation, tuning, explanations, error analysis, conformal ranges), regression, neural networks, time series, saved models, model health and monitoring.
  • Learn: a concept lab of simulations and a bilingual glossary with reading guides.
  • Share: panels, HTML and PDF reports, Excel, notebooks and single-file projects.
  • Advanced: text, customers, impact, recommendations, surveys, networks, geography, model governance and synthetic data.

docs.title: API server
docs.text:
kikolens api serves the analysis over HTTP and JSON, so other programs (a web app, a spreadsheet macro, a scheduler, another language) can use it. It runs on your machine, keeps everything in memory and sends nothing anywhere. It needs nothing beyond KikoLens.

kikolens api                                    # http://127.0.0.1:8000
kikolens api --token s3cret --host 0.0.0.0      # reachable from the network: a token is mandatory
kikolens api --data-dir ./data --model my-model --cors http://localhost:3000

Open /openapi.json for the machine-readable description and /functions for the analyses and their parameters. The older kikolens serve MODEL is still there for serving one model only.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• It listens only on this computer unless you pass another --host, and then --token is required (Authorization: Bearer TOKEN; /health is open).
  • Clients can only run a fixed list of analyses. They cannot run code, read arbitrary paths or run arbitrary SQL (queries are read-only and cannot open files).
  • Files can be loaded only by name from the folder given with --data-dir; without it, clients send rows or csv text. Names that escape the folder are refused.
  • At most 20 datasets of a million rows are held at once, request bodies are limited to 25 MB, and unexpected errors are reported by type only, never with paths or stack traces.
  • --model opens a saved model file, which is code: serve only models you trust. Only the models you name are served.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Call What it does GET /health {"status": "ok"}. GET /functions The analyses: name, description, parameters. POST /datasets Create a dataset from {"rows": [{...}]}, {"csv": "a,b\n1,2"} or {"file": "sales.csv"}; optional "name". Returns its id. GET /datasets, GET /datasets/{id} List them, or see columns, types, missing values and the first rows. DELETE /datasets/{id} Forget a dataset. POST /run/{function} {"dataset": id, "args": {...}}. Runs the analysis and returns {"result": {"summary": ..., "table": {"columns", "rows", "total_rows"}, ...}, "omitted": [...]}. Add ?figures=1 for charts as Plotly JSON. Tables are cut to 200 rows. POST /jobs, GET /jobs/{id} The same in the background for slow work (lab, autopilot): {"function", "dataset", "args"} returns an id; poll until status is done or failed. GET /models, POST /models/{name}/predict The models named at startup; send {"rows": [...]} and get predictions with ranges and input warnings.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import requests
base = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
rows = [{"price": 10, "units": 100}, {"price": 12, "units": 90}]  # ...more rows
dataset = requests.post(f"{base}/datasets", json={"rows": rows}).json()["id"]
out = requests.post(f"{base}/run/regress", json={"dataset": dataset, "args": {"target": "units"}}).json()
print(out["result"]["summary"])

Status codes: 400 for an invalid request or arguments (the message says why), 401 for a missing or wrong token, 404 for an unknown dataset, function, job or model, 409 when too many datasets are held, 413 for a body that is too large.

First stable release. KikoLens is a private, local-first data analysis workbench: the data never leaves your machine, and the optional language-model features run on a local Ollama server.

  • Data: loading from files, links, Google Sheets, object storage and SQL databases; a quality score with undoable fixes; detection and masking of personal data with k-anonymity; fuzzy joins; replayable recipes with a safe formula interpreter; a one-click autopilot; an analyst that chats with the data using validated specifications.
  • Analysis: automatic choice of statistical tests, classical, Bayesian and always-valid sequential A/B tests with CUPED and split checks, anomaly detection, PCA and t-SNE, drift, clustering, "why did this figure change", survival, and causal inference (propensity, matching, doubly robust, uplift, regression discontinuity, synthetic control, instrumental variables).
  • Models: a model lab with cross-validation against a baseline, tuning, leak detection, Shapley values, error analysis, decision thresholds and conformal ranges; regression with inference; a neural network in scikit-learn or PyTorch; time series (backtested forecasts, ADF / KPSS / STL / ARIMA); versioned model packages that warn about unfamiliar data; model health, governance and monitoring.
  • Learn: a concept lab with eight simulations and a bilingual glossary with a reading guide for the main sections.
  • Advanced: text mining, customers and cohorts, impact of a change, recommendations, surveys, networks, geography and synthetic data.
  • Share: a panel with cross-filtering, HTML and PDF reports, a formatted Excel workbook, a Jupyter notebook of the session and a single-file project.
  • Everywhere: the dashboard (English and Spanish, light and dark), a command line, a Python API with Jupyter magics, a small model server and a local JSON API server.
  • Engineering: unit and end-to-end tests, CI on Windows, Linux and macOS with pandas 2 and 3, CodeQL, a Docker image and a documentation site.

docs.title: Command line reference
docs.text: Every command accepts a local file, an http(s) link or a database URI (sqlite:///data.db, postgresql://user:pass@host/db) wherever it says SOURCE.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: Command What it does kikolens start [--port N] Launch the dashboard. kikolens analyze SOURCE Statistics for every column and the data quality summary. --no-quality skips the latter. kikolens sql SOURCE "QUERY" Run a read-only SQL query. The data is the table df. kikolens ask SOURCE "QUESTION" [--model NAME] A local model writes the SQL, then it runs. Needs Ollama. kikolens clean SOURCE --output FILE [--save-recipe FILE] Apply the safe automatic cleaning and save as .csv or .parquet. --save-recipe also writes the steps as a JSON recipe. kikolens apply SOURCE RECIPE --output FILE [-d PATH] Repeat a recipe on another file. -d PATH (or -d name=PATH) supplies the extra datasets that join steps need; it can be repeated. Without a name, the file's name is used, which is how the dashboard names uploaded files. kikolens validate SOURCE [RULES.json] [--save FILE] Check the data against validation rules (or the rules suggested by the data). Exit code 2 when a rule is broken. kikolens export SOURCE OUTPUT [--recipe FILE] [--workbook] Convert to .csv, .tsv, .xlsx, .json, .ndjson, .parquet or .feather. --workbook makes a formatted Excel workbook with quality, statistics and recipe sheets. kikolens to-db SOURCE DATABASE TABLE [--if-exists fail\|append\|replace] Write the data into a table. It never overwrites unless you say replace. kikolens autopilot SOURCE [--target COL] [--horizon N] [--thorough] [--clean FILE] [--recipe FILE] [--pdf FILE] A first full analysis: clean, find patterns, model a column and forecast dates. --clean and --recipe save the cleaned data and the steps; --pdf writes a report. kikolens privacy SOURCE [--scan] [--mask a,b] [--hash a,b] [--drop a,b] [--salt S] [--output FILE] [--recipe FILE] [--k N --quasi a,b] Find personal data, mask / hash / remove columns and measure k-anonymity. The salt used by --hash is written to the recipe, so keep the recipe private. kikolens dictionary SOURCE [--output FILE.md\|.csv\|.xlsx] Describe every column: meaning, empty share, typical values, ranges and warnings. kikolens notebook SOURCE OUTPUT.ipynb [--recipe FILE] [--target COL] [--exclude a,b] [--date COL --value COL] [--horizon N] Write a Jupyter notebook that reproduces the analysis. kikolens link LEFT RIGHT LEFT_COLUMN RIGHT_COLUMN [--threshold 0.85] [--output FILE] Match records whose names are not spelled the same way. kikolens run PIPELINE.json Run a pipeline file (see below). Exit code 2 when a fail_on condition triggers, 1 when something cannot be read. kikolens jupyter [FOLDER] [--no-open] Write a quickstart notebook for the Python API and open it in JupyterLab if it is installed. See the Python API guide. kikolens fit SOURCE COLUMN [--only normal,gamma] Which distribution describes a numeric column best (AIC, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, normality). kikolens segment SOURCE [gmm\|hierarchical\|dbscan] [--columns a,b] [--groups 4] [--output FILE] Segment rows and describe each group in words; --output adds a group column. kikolens recommend SOURCE USER ITEM [--rating COL] [--for PERSON] [--similar-to ITEM] [--evaluate] Item-based recommender from a table of who used what. kikolens synth SOURCE OUTPUT [--rows N] [--seed N] [--report] Generate synthetic data with the same distributions and correlations; --report measures fidelity and privacy. kikolens analyst SOURCE "QUESTION" [--model M] [--no-samples] [--html FILE] [--trail FILE.py] Ask a question in your own words: a local model decides whether to draw a chart, run SQL or chain analyses, and every step is shown. --trail writes the steps as Python code. Needs Ollama; without it a basic analysis is chosen from keywords. kikolens chart SOURCE "REQUEST" [--output chart.html\|spec.json] Describe a chart in words; the model writes a specification that KikoLens validates and draws. kikolens classify-text SOURCE COLUMN --labels a,b,c [--output FILE] [--limit 300] Classify a text column into labels you choose, without training anything. kikolens project FILE.kikolens [--output FILE] Show what a project contains (notes, recipe) and optionally export its processed data.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Command What it does kikolens predict SOURCE TARGET Train AutoML on TARGET and print metrics and top features. kikolens predict SOURCE TARGET --nn [--layers "64, 32"] Same, with a neural network. kikolens lab SOURCE TARGET Compare many models with cross-validation, tune the best one and check for data leaks. kikolens score SOURCE MODEL [--output FILE] [--raw] Predict a file with a saved model. MODEL is a .klmodel path or the name of a saved model. --raw repeats the cleaning steps the model was trained with first. kikolens models List the saved models. kikolens models info NAME [--card FILE] Metrics and expected columns of a model; --card writes a Markdown model card. kikolens models compare SOURCE MODEL MODEL [MODEL...] Which of several saved models predicts better on data whose real results are known, and whether the gap is reliable. kikolens governance Every registered model with its stage, owner, risk, latest validation and whether a review is due. kikolens governance register MODEL --owner NAME [--description T] [--intended-use T] [--limitations T] [--risk low\|medium\|high] Register a saved model (it starts as a draft). governance update changes the card. kikolens governance validate MODEL DATA [--max-drop 0.2] Test on rows with known results and record whether it holds up. kikolens governance checks MODEL STAGE / promote MODEL STAGE [--data DATA] [--reason T] [--force] See what blocks a move, or make it. Moving to production replaces and archives the current production model of the same target. kikolens governance approve MODEL --actor NAME / rollback TARGET Approve this version of a model; go back to the previous production model. kikolens governance card MODEL [--output FILE] / audit [MODEL] The model card in Markdown; verify the audit log chain and show the latest entries. kikolens models delete NAME Remove a saved model. kikolens forecast SOURCE DATE VALUE [--horizon N] [--freq D] [--agg mean] Forecast a numeric column. Frequencies: h, D, W, MS, QS, YS. kikolens forecast ... --compare Compare five models with rolling-origin tests and forecast with the best one. kikolens forecast ... --changes Also list level shifts and trend changes in the series. kikolens forecast ... --by COLUMN One forecast per value of a column (the 20 with the most activity). kikolens serve MODEL [--port 8000] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--token T] Serve a saved model as a small JSON API. POST /predict with {"rows": [{...}]} returns predictions and warnings; GET /model describes the inputs; GET /health. It listens only on this computer unless you give another --host, which requires --token (sent as Authorization: Bearer T). kikolens api [--port 8000] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--token T] [--data-dir DIR] [--model NAME] [--cors ORIGIN] The whole toolkit as a JSON API: datasets, analyses, background jobs, and models. See API server.

predict and lab take --save PATH to write a model package to a file and --register NAME to keep it with your saved models. lab also takes --folds, --no-tune, --bayes (Bayesian optimisation instead of a random search), --models "Ridge,Random Forest", --balance and --exclude col1,col2. Besides the default models, --models accepts SVM, AdaBoost, Bagging, Voting Ensemble, Stacking Ensemble and, with PyTorch installed, PyTorch MLP.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Command What it does kikolens anomalies SOURCE [--method M] [--share 2] [--columns a,b] [--output FILE] Flag the most unusual rows and say why. Methods: Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, Robust z-score, Mahalanobis distance. kikolens screen SOURCE TARGET Test every column against TARGET and list those reliably related to it, corrected for testing many columns. kikolens ab SOURCE GROUP OUTCOME --control VALUE [--success VALUE] Compare a control and a treatment group on rates or averages. kikolens drift REFERENCE CURRENT [--output FILE] Compare two datasets column by column. Exits with code 2 when the data changed a lot, so it works as an alarm in scripts and CI. kikolens text SOURCE COLUMN [--group COL] [--ngram 1\|2\|3] [--themes K] Key terms of a free-text column, the terms that distinguish each group, and themes. kikolens topics SOURCE COLUMN [--topics N] [--method nmf\|lda] [--date COL] Topics in a text column; the number is chosen by coherence unless given. With --date, how each topic changes over time. kikolens near-duplicates SOURCE COLUMN [--threshold 0.9] / similar SOURCE COLUMN "a phrase" [--n 5] Groups of near-identical texts; the texts most like a phrase. kikolens patterns SOURCE COLUMN [--kinds email,url,...] Emails, links, phones, amounts, percentages, dates, hashtags and mentions. kikolens keyphrases SOURCE COLUMN / readability SOURCE COLUMN Key phrases (RAKE); reading ease per text. kikolens network FILE SOURCE TARGET [--weight COL] [--directed] [--output FILE] Important nodes, communities and connectivity of a network given as a list of links. kikolens network-path FILE SOURCE TARGET START END / suggest-links FILE SOURCE TARGET / network-robustness FILE SOURCE TARGET The shortest path between two nodes; the links that are probably missing; how the network breaks when hubs are removed. kikolens geo-check FILE [--lat COL --lon COL] Which rows have usable coordinates and what looks wrong (swapped, out of range, 0,0, repeated). kikolens geo-distances FILE --point LAT,LON or --centers FILE [--center-name COL] [--reach-km N] Kilometres to a place or to the nearest centre, and how many points each centre serves. kikolens geo-hotspots FILE [--value COL] [--eps-km 5] [--min-points 10] Dense zones of points. kikolens spatial FILE VALUE [--k 8] Moran's I and Getis-Ord hot and cold spots for a numeric column. kikolens geo-grid FILE [--value COL] [--cell-km 10] [--agg mean] Summary by square cells. kikolens panel SOURCE [PANEL.json] [--where "region in North,West"] [--output FILE] [--save FILE] Build a one-page panel of metrics, charts and tables as a web page; without a definition, one is suggested from the data. --where keeps only matching rows and can be repeated. kikolens report SOURCE [--target COL] [--nn] [--ai] [--output FILE] [--pdf FILE] Build the HTML report, and a PDF with --pdf. kikolens survival SOURCE DURATION EVENT [--group COL] Kaplan-Meier medians and a log-rank test between groups. kikolens cohorts SOURCE USER DATE [--period Day\|Week\|Month] Retention by cohort. kikolens rfm SOURCE CUSTOMER DATE AMOUNT [--output FILE] Recency, frequency and spend segments. --output writes every customer with their segment. kikolens basket SOURCE TRANSACTION ITEM [--support 0.02] [--confidence 0.3] Association rules: what is bought together. kikolens impact SOURCE DATE VALUE --at YYYY-MM-DD [--control a,b] [--agg mean\|sum] Estimate the effect of a change against what would have happened. kikolens regress SOURCE TARGET [--using a,b] [--positive VALUE] [--output FILE] Linear regression for a number and logistic for a two-valued column: coefficients with ranges and p-values, each effect in a sentence, and warnings about collinearity or unreliable errors. kikolens spikes SOURCE DATE VALUE [--agg mean\|sum] [--sensitivity 3.5] [--output FILE] Unusual periods in a series once trend and season are taken out. kikolens why SOURCE DATE [--metric COL] [--agg sum\|mean\|count] [--before START,END] [--after START,END] [--by a,b] Explain why a figure changed between two periods: which values of which columns account for it. The end date is not included; by default it compares the last third of the dates with the one before. kikolens ab-seq SOURCE GROUP OUTCOME CONTROL [--order COL] [--alpha 0.05] Sequential A/B test (mSPRT): valid even if you look after every observation. kikolens bandit RATES [--visitors N] Simulate a Thompson-sampling bandit against an even split. kikolens granger SOURCE DATE CAUSE EFFECT [--max-lag 7] Does the past of one column help predict another? Predictive, not proof of cause. kikolens effect SOURCE TREATMENT OUTCOME [--covariates a,b] [--method aipw\|regression\|ipw\|matching] [--treated-value V] Causal effect of a treatment, adjusting for confounders, with the raw difference, balance and overlap warnings and an E-value. kikolens uplift SOURCE TREATMENT OUTCOME [--covariates a,b] Who responds most to a treatment: effect by decile and a Qini curve. kikolens discontinuity SOURCE RUNNING OUTCOME CUTOFF [--bandwidth H] Effect of crossing a threshold, with a bandwidth sweep and a manipulation test. kikolens synth-control SOURCE UNIT TIME OUTCOME TREATED_UNIT INTERVENTION Effect on one unit against a weighted mix of control units, with placebo tests. kikolens iv SOURCE OUTCOME ENDOGENOUS --instruments z1,z2 [--covariates a,b] Instrumental variables (two-stage least squares) with a first-stage strength check. kikolens likert FILE --items a,b [--reverse c] / reliability FILE --items a,b,c Scale questions (favourable share, mean, spread); Cronbach's alpha and what each question contributes. kikolens nps FILE SCORE [--group COL] / crosstab FILE ROW COLUMN Net Promoter Score with its interval; a cross-tab with residuals and Cramér's V. kikolens key-drivers FILE OUTCOME --items a,b,c / survey-groups FILE GROUP --items a,b / response-quality FILE --items a,b,... What matters most for an overall rating; which questions differ between groups; straight-liners and blanks. kikolens learn [CONCEPT] [--set name=value] [--seed N] [--figure FILE] The concept lab: without a name it lists the concepts; with one it runs the simulation and prints what it shows, the lesson and what to try. kikolens glossary [TERM] [--lang en\|es] Define a term with what to watch out for; give a word to search the glossary; no argument lists every term. kikolens forecast-drivers SOURCE DATE TARGET --drivers a,b [--scenario price=1.1] [--horizon N] Forecast a column using other columns too, and test whether they help. kikolens stationarity SOURCE DATE VALUE [--trend] ADF and KPSS together, and how many differences the series needs. kikolens acf SOURCE DATE VALUE [--nlags N] Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation with the Ljung-Box test. kikolens stl SOURCE DATE VALUE [--period N] [--output FILE] Robust trend, seasonal and remainder, with the strength of each. kikolens arima SOURCE DATE VALUE [--order p,d,q] [--seasonal P,D,Q] [--period N] [--horizon N] Seasonal ARIMA forecast with ranges and diagnostics; without --order the best model is searched by AICc. kikolens select-features SOURCE TARGET [--exclude a,b] [--output FILE] Which columns are worth keeping: consensus of four methods and a cross-validated curve. kikolens runs [--target COL] [--best] [--compare id,id] [--delete id] The history of model lab runs. kikolens ab-bayes SOURCE GROUP OUTCOME CONTROL [--success VALUE] Bayesian A/B: the probability a variant is better and the cost of choosing wrongly. kikolens experiment FILE GROUP OUTCOME CONTROL [--pre COL] [--date COL] [--segments a,b] [--expected control=50,new=50] Full A/B analysis: split check, effect of each group against the control (CUPED with --pre), effect over time and by segment, and a verdict. kikolens srm FILE GROUP [--expected a=50,b=50] / cuped FILE GROUP OUTCOME PRE CONTROL Only the split check; only the noise reduction. kikolens features SOURCE TARGET [--max-new 5] [--apply FILE] [--recipe FILE] Search for ratios, products and other new columns that improve a model; --apply writes the data with them and --recipe the steps.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Command What it does kikolens performance SOURCE MODEL [--date COL] [--period Day\|Week\|Month\|Quarter] [--raw] Is a saved model still good? Scores newer data whose real results are known, period by period, against the accuracy it had in testing. Exit code 2 on a warning. kikolens monitor create NAME SOURCE [--baseline DATA] [--recipe FILE] [--model NAME] [--rules FILE] [--webhook URL] [--drift-level high\|medium] [--quality-drop 10] Create a monitor. The baseline (the source as it is now, unless you give another) is stored inside the monitor. kikolens monitor run NAME [--source FILE] One check. Exit code 0 fine or warnings only, 2 alerts, 1 the data could not be read. kikolens monitor list / history NAME [--last N] The monitors and the past checks of one. kikolens monitor watch NAME [--interval 300] Keep running and check whenever the watched file changes. kikolens monitor schedule NAME [--every hourly\|daily\|weekly] Print the cron and Windows commands that run the check on a schedule. Nothing is installed. kikolens monitor delete NAME Remove a monitor and its history.

A check records rows, quality score, drift against the baseline, broken rules and the model's predictions, and raises alerts for: drift at or above the chosen level, a quality drop, a change of 50% or more in rows, columns missing from or added to the data, columns that changed from numbers to text, model inputs outside the training range, and a shift of 20% in the average prediction (or 10 points in the classifier's confidence). If a webhook is configured it receives a short JSON summary, only when a check ends in alert or failed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
kikolens analyze examples/sales_demo.csv
kikolens sql examples/sales_demo.csv "SELECT region, ROUND(SUM(revenue)) AS total FROM df GROUP BY region ORDER BY total DESC"
kikolens clean examples/sales_demo.csv --output clean.csv --save-recipe recipe.json
kikolens lab clean.csv revenue --folds 5 --register sales-model
kikolens apply examples/sales_new_quarter.csv recipe.json --output new_clean.csv
kikolens score new_clean.csv sales-model --output predictions.csv
kikolens drift clean.csv new_clean.csv --output drift.csv
kikolens anomalies clean.csv --share 1 --output odd_rows.csv
kikolens monitor create sales-feed clean.csv --model sales-model --recipe recipe.json
kikolens monitor run sales-feed --source examples/sales_new_quarter.csv
kikolens text examples/reviews.csv review --group product --themes 3
kikolens forecast clean.csv date revenue --horizon 30 --compare --changes
kikolens export clean.csv analysis.xlsx --workbook
kikolens report examples/sales_demo.csv --target revenue --nn --output report.html

docs.title: Recipes and model packages
docs.text:
A recipe (.json) is the ordered list of cleaning and transformation steps. It has no data in it and can be applied to any file with the same columns. A model package (.klmodel) holds a trained model together with the columns it expects, their training ranges, its classes and its test metrics. Saved models live in ~/.kikolens/models (change it with KIKOLENS_HOME); saving the same name again creates a new version (-v2, -v3).

score prints warnings before it predicts: columns that are missing, values that could not be read, categories never seen in training and numbers far outside the training range. Regression models also write a likely range (<target>_low, <target>_high), and classifiers write confidence and one probability column per class.

Model packages are pickles: only open files you created or trust.

docs.title: Pipeline files
docs.text:
kikolens run reads a JSON file that says what to do with a dataset and where to leave the results; paths are relative to the file. Only source is required.

{
  "source": "today.csv",
  "recipe": "recipe.json",
  "rules": "rules.json",
  "baseline": "training.csv",
  "model": "sales-model",
  "min_quality": 80,
  "outputs": {"data": "out/clean.csv", "predictions": "out/scored.csv", "report": "out/report.html", "log": "out/log.json"},
  "fail_on": ["rules", "drift", "quality", "input"]
}

The stages run in this order: read, apply the recipe, score the quality, validate the rules, compare with the baseline (which also goes through the recipe), score with the model, write the outputs. A problem is only fatal if its name is in fail_on (rules: a rule is broken; drift: the data drifted a lot; quality: the score is below min_quality; input: the model received columns or values it did not see in training); otherwise it is shown as a warning. The log output is a JSON record of the run. Typical use is a daily job: kikolens run pipeline.json || notify-someone.

docs.title: SQL safety
docs.text: Only a single read-only statement runs. These are rejected: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, CREATE, ALTER, ATTACH, COPY, PRAGMA, several statements separated by ;, and file-reading functions such as read_csv(...). Comments and text inside quotes are ignored when checking.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose OLLAMA_HOST http://localhost:11434 Where Ollama is running. OLLAMA_MODEL llama3.2 Model for ask, summaries and report commentary. OLLAMA_TIMEOUT 120 Seconds to wait for the model. KIKOLENS_HOME ~/.kikolens Folder for saved models (models/) and monitors (monitors/).

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: 0 success. 1 a file cannot be loaded, a column does not exist, a query is rejected, a model cannot be trained or found, or a recipe fails; the reason is printed. 2 from drift when the data changed a lot, from validate when a rule is broken, and from monitor run when a check raises an alert.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
KikoLens works without any configuration. These are the ways to change its behaviour, from the strongest to the weakest.

  1. Environment variables
  2. kikolens.toml in the folder you run KikoLens from
  3. config.toml in your KikoLens folder (~/.kikolens, or the folder in KIKOLENS_HOME)
  4. The defaults

A file that is not valid TOML, a value of the wrong type, or a key that is not known never stops KikoLens from starting: it is ignored, and kikolens doctor lists the problem.

[ollama]
host = "http://localhost:11434"   # where Ollama is listening
model = "llama3.2"                # the model used to write SQL, summaries and commentary
timeout = 120                     # seconds to wait for an answer

[dashboard]
port = 8501                       # `kikolens start` uses this unless you pass --port
language = "es"                   # "en" or "es": the language the dashboard opens in

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Meaning OLLAMA_HOST, OLLAMA_MODEL, OLLAMA_TIMEOUT The same as the [ollama] keys. KIKOLENS_HOME Where saved models, monitors, run history and config.toml live. Default ~/.kikolens.

docs.title: Check everything
docs.text:
kikolens doctor             # versions, optional extras, the user folder, Ollama and the configuration
kikolens doctor --offline   # skip the Ollama check
kikolens doctor --json      # machine-readable

It exits with code 1 if something required is missing or too old, so it can be used in a script or a container health check.

docs.title: Measure speed
docs.text:
kikolens benchmark --rows 20000
kikolens benchmark --rows 100000 --only "model lab,forecast" --repeat 3 --output bench.json

Times profiling, cleaning, SQL, drift, anomaly detection, a forecast, a three-model lab run, the data story and synthetic data on generated data. Useful to spot a regression and to know what to expect with a big file.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text: Extra Adds kikolens[torch] The PyTorch network in the model lab. kikolens[jupyter] JupyterLab, for kikolens jupyter. kikolens[cloud] s3:// and gs:// sources. kikolens[postgres], kikolens[mysql] Those databases. kikolens[docs] Playwright, to regenerate the screenshots.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text: kikolens --install-completion installs tab completion for your shell.

docs.title: Dashboard guide
docs.text:
Start it with kikolens start and open http://localhost:8501. Pick a file, a link or a database in the sidebar; every section works on the same dataset, and the cleaning and transformation steps carry over to the rest.

The sidebar has two levels: an area (Data, Analysis, Models, Learn, Share and Advanced) and, under it, the sections of that area. The interface follows the light or dark theme from Streamlit's settings menu (top right). The Go to box at the top of the sidebar jumps straight to any section by name (there are about fifty). The Language / Idioma menu at the bottom of the sidebar switches the fixed texts (sections, buttons, labels, help) to Spanish. Messages that report results, such as the sentences a test writes about your data, stay in English.

docs.title: Loading data
docs.text: The sidebar's Source menu offers four ways in: File (CSV, TSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet; for an Excel book with several sheets you pick the sheet), URL (any link to those formats, a Google Sheet shared so that anyone with the link can view it, and s3:// or gs:// addresses when the cloud extra is installed), Paste (copy cells from a spreadsheet or a web page, header row included; the separator is detected) and Database (SQLite, PostgreSQL or MySQL: pick a table, or type a read-only query).

docs.title: Home, data story and chart gallery
docs.text:
Home is the first thing you see after loading data: a quality ring, how many columns of each kind there are, a strip showing where the empty values are, a small chart for every numeric column (and the trend over time if there is a date), the things worth a look, and one-click buttons to the autopilot, the cleaning page and the story. With no data loaded, the welcome screen offers four built-in examples (sales, reviews, orders and subscriptions) so you can try everything at once.

Data story reads the data like an analyst and tells it in short chapters, each with its sentence, key figures and a chart: what is there, quality, what stands out, what moves together, how the main numeric column evolves (with its unusual periods marked), which groups differ most, the unusual rows, and where to go next. Download it as Markdown.

Chart gallery has nine charts a bar chart cannot replace: a Sankey diagram of the flow between two columns, a treemap of nested groups, a radar chart of each group's profile, correlations reordered so similar columns sit together, a network of correlated columns, a calendar of activity, ridgelines of a distribution by group, parallel coordinates, and one panel per group.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Rows, columns, quality score, missing cells and memory use, a table with the type and health of every column, and a preview of the data.

docs.title: Autopilot
docs.text: A first full analysis in one click, for when you open a file and do not know where to start. It cleans with the safe fixes (as recipe steps you can apply to your data), classifies the columns (dates, identifiers, free text, categories, numbers), looks for strong relationships and dominant categories, picks a column to predict from typical names such as target, revenue or churn (or the one you choose), compares a few models against a baseline, and, if there is a date column, forecasts the series. Each phase that cannot run says why and the others continue. It ends with a written summary and concrete next steps. Thorough compares every model and tunes the best, which takes longer.

docs.title: Explore
docs.text: Pick a chart type and the columns to plot. Filters (numeric range, date range, category) narrow the rows first. Scatter and density charts sample 20,000 points so they stay responsive.

docs.title: Quality and cleaning
docs.text:
Lists everything wrong with the data, ordered by how much it matters:

  • missing values and columns that are mostly empty
  • duplicated rows
  • constant columns
  • text columns that are really numbers, dates or booleans
  • outliers (IQR rule)

Auto-clean applies only the safe fixes: trim whitespace, drop duplicates, convert mistyped columns, drop constant columns. Everything else is an explicit operation you choose. Undo reverts the last action (Auto-clean counts as one) and Reset returns to the file as loaded. The original file is never modified.

The Missing data patterns, Near-duplicate rows and Validation rules tabs under the cleaning tools go further:

  • Missing data patterns tells you which columns are empty together and, more importantly, whether the gaps are random. When the chance of a gap depends on another column (for example, income is missing mostly for one region) filling it with a single typical value would bias the results, and the page says so.
  • Smart fill (in the operation list) fills gaps with KNN (from the most similar rows), iterative (predicting each gap from the other columns) or by group (the median or most common value of each group). It can add a column that marks the filled cells.
  • Merge similar spellings unifies New York, new york, NewYork and New Yrok into the most common form, after showing you what it would merge.
  • Near-duplicate rows finds pairs that are almost, but not exactly, the same (a typo in a name, a different case) and lets you remove the ones you confirm.
  • Validation rules are checks written by whoever knows the data: not empty, unique, a range, allowed values, a pattern, "end date is not before start date", "not in the future". KikoLens can suggest rules from the current data, shows which rows break each rule, and saves them as JSON for kikolens validate and for monitors.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Finds the columns that hold personal data and lets you decide what to do with each: keep it, mask it (everything but the last two characters), replace it with a salted SHA-256 fingerprint (equal values keep equal fingerprints, so counts and joins still work, but the original cannot be recovered) or remove the column. Detection looks at the content with validated patterns (email, phone, IP address, credit card with its check digit, IBAN with its check, Spanish DNI/NIE with its letter, US social security number) and at column names such as name or birth. The steps go into the recipe. The second tab, How identifiable, measures k-anonymity: for the columns that describe a person (age, postal code, sex, city...) it shows the size of the smallest group a person hides in, how many rows are in a group smaller than the k you want, and the groups that stand out.

docs.title: Match records
docs.text: Joins two tables whose names are not spelled the same way (accents, word order, typos). Upload the second file, pick the name columns and a minimum similarity; every row of the open data gets its best partner if one is good enough. Matches that are not exact are listed for review, and those with a close runner-up are flagged. One click adds the partner's columns (ending in _right) and the score, and it can be undone.

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
Six tabs of operations, each recorded as a step:

Tab Operations Rows Filter by a condition (==, >, in, contains, is empty...), sort, sample a fraction or a number of rows. Columns Create a column from a formula, combine or split text, rename, replace values. Features Date parts (year, month, weekday, weekend, days since start), bins by quantile or equal width, scaling (standard, min-max, robust), log, rank, one-hot encoding. Sequences Lagged values and rolling statistics, ordered by a column and optionally within a group (for example per customer). Reshape Group and summarize, pivot, stack columns. Combine Upload a second file and join it on a key (left, inner, outer, right) or append its rows.

Formulas accept column names, numbers, + - * / // % **, comparisons and the functions log, log1p, log10, sqrt, abs, exp, round, floor, ceil, min, max. Put a name with spaces between backticks: log1p(`unit price`). Division by zero gives an empty value, not an error. Anything else is rejected, so a recipe from someone else cannot run code.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: Correlations above 0.85, columns with extreme values, categories that dominate, and probable identifier columns. A button asks the local language model for a written summary (needs Ollama).

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: A summary table, the distribution of any column, and the correlation matrix with the ten strongest relationships.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text: Type a question and a local model writes the SQL; you can edit it before it runs. The SQL tab runs your own queries. The data is the table df. Only read-only queries are accepted.

docs.title: Analyst
docs.text:
A chat with your data, answered by a language model that runs on this computer (Ollama). Ask in your own words and the analyst decides what to do:

  • "Show the total revenue by region in 2024" draws a chart. The model does not write code: it describes the chart (kind, columns, aggregation, time grain, filters, top N) in a small specification that KikoLens checks against your columns and draws itself. If the specification is wrong ("column turnover does not exist, the columns are..."), that sentence goes back to the model so it can correct it.
  • "How many rows per region?" runs a read-only SQL query (validated like in Ask).
  • "Why did revenue fall in the last quarter?" hands over to an analysis agent that chains KikoLens tools (regression, forecast, why it changed, unusual periods, segments, survival, Granger, RFM...), one at a time. Each choice is validated (the tool and every column must exist), run, and summarised back to the model, up to five steps, and every step is shown with its reason. Download the trail as Markdown, or as Python code that repeats the same calls without the model.

The model only ever chooses and explains; every number comes from the analyses. If Ollama is not running, the page says so and falls back to a basic analysis picked from keywords in your question. Settings lets you stop sending sample values of the data to the model (only column names, types and ranges); it all stays on this computer either way.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Six tabs that answer "is this real or chance?" in plain language. Each result shows the test used, the p-value, the effect size with a label (negligible, small, medium, large) and a conclusion that also says what you cannot conclude.

  • Compare groups. Pick a number and a column that splits the rows. Two groups: Welch's t-test, or Mann-Whitney when the data are clearly not normal. Three or more: ANOVA with Tukey comparisons, or Kruskal-Wallis with Holm-adjusted comparisons. The page tells you which was chosen and why.
  • Two categories. Chi-squared test (Fisher's exact for small 2x2 tables) with Cramér's V and a map of where the table departs from chance.
  • Correlation. Pearson and Spearman with a confidence interval, and a warning when outliers or curvature distort the picture.
  • A/B test. Control against treatment on a rate (two-proportion z-test and the probability that the treatment is better) or an average (Welch). Includes a planner that tells you how many rows each group needs before you start.
  • A/B (Bayesian). The same comparison without a p-value: the probability that the variant is better, the likely difference and relative lift with their ranges, and the expected loss of choosing wrongly.
  • What relates to... Tests every column against a target and corrects for running many tests at once (Benjamini-Hochberg), so a handful of random "hits" are not reported as findings.

Is the test sound? (the last tab) reads an A/B test the careful way. It first checks that each group got the share of users that was planned (a sample ratio mismatch, which usually means a bug and invalidates the test; if it fails, the page refuses to name a winner). It then gives the effect of every group against the control with its 95 % range (several variants are corrected with Holm), uses an earlier measure of the same outcome to remove noise (CUPED) and shows how much narrower the range becomes, plots the effect week by week and warns when it is fading or growing, and looks for segments whose effect differs from the rest of the rows, corrected for the number of segments examined. When nothing is significant it tells you the smallest effect the test could have found, so a small real effect is not mistaken for no effect.

docs.title: Sequential tests
docs.text: A/B tests that stay valid however often you look. A classic test is only right if you check once, at the end; checking daily and stopping when it looks significant multiplies the false positives. The live test uses a mixture sequential probability ratio test (mSPRT): it shows the evidence building up as visitors arrive, tells you when it is enough to stop, and gives an always-valid p-value and range next to the (misleading if peeked at) classic p-value. The planner simulates how many visitors the sequential test needs against a fixed-size test, and how often it raises a false alarm when there is no effect. The bandit simulator shows how a Thompson-sampling bandit shifts traffic to the winning variant while it learns, and how many more conversions that gives than an even split.

docs.title: Anomalies
docs.text: Choose columns, a method and the share of rows to flag. Methods: Isolation Forest (general purpose), Local Outlier Factor (odd rows inside dense groups), Robust z-score (one column at a time, easiest to explain) and Mahalanobis distance (accounts for correlated columns). Every flagged row comes with the reason, such as "income is 8.2 robust SDs above typical". You can download the rows or remove them (undoable; removal is not stored in the recipe, because the rows are specific to this data).

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text:
• PCA. How many components capture 90% of the variation, what each is made of, and a scatter of the rows on any two components, colored by a column.
  • t-SNE. A 2D map where similar rows sit together (a sample of 3,000 rows is used on larger data).
  • Redundant columns. The variance inflation factor of each column: above 5 it is largely explained by the others, above 10 it is nearly a duplicate.

docs.title: Distribution fit
docs.text: Which distribution describes a numeric column best: normal, lognormal, exponential, gamma, Weibull, beta, uniform, Laplace or Student t, ranked by AIC with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, the histogram with the fitted curve, and a Q-Q plot against the best one. Distributions that cannot hold the data (a lognormal for negative values) are left out, and the page says whether the column looks normal.

docs.title: Compare data
docs.text: See what changed between two datasets: the first part of the data against the rest, the original file against your working data, or another file against the open one. Each column gets a verdict (stable, moderate, drift) from the population stability index (PSI), a KS or chi-squared test, and notes such as new categories or a changed share of empty values. Dates and columns that are different in every row (identifiers) are shown as info, since they are expected to change. Text that holds numbers or dates (1,200, 2024-03-01) is read as such. Columns that exist in only one dataset, or changed from numbers to text, are called out. Use it to check whether new data still looks like what a model was trained on.

docs.title: Segments
docs.text: k-means clustering on the numeric columns, with an optional chart of inertia and silhouette scores to help choose the number of groups. Download the data with the segment label attached.

docs.title: Why it changed
docs.text: A figure moved between two periods; which regions, channels or products explain it? Pick the date column, whether to measure a total, an average or the number of rows, and the two periods (by default the last third of the dates against the one before). The page ranks the columns by how much of the change sits in their single biggest value, draws a waterfall of what moved it for any column, and, for totals and counts, lists the combinations of two columns that moved most. For an average the change is split into a mix effect (the weight of a value changed) and a rate effect (the average inside the value changed).

docs.title: Causal effect
docs.text: Did a treatment really change an outcome, or do the treated rows simply differ from the rest? Five tabs. Effect of a treatment compares the raw difference with regression, inverse-propensity weighting, matching and a doubly robust estimator (cross-fitted, with bootstrap ranges), and shows the overlap of propensities, the covariate balance before and after weighting and an E-value: how strong an unmeasured factor would have to be to explain the result away. Who responds most estimates the effect per row with two models (one per group), ranks rows by predicted uplift and draws a Qini curve against random targeting. Threshold estimates the jump where a rule kicks in (a score cut-off, an age limit) with local regression, several bandwidths and a test for rows piling up on one side. Synthetic control builds a weighted mix of other units that follows the treated one before the intervention and runs placebo tests on every control unit. Instrument runs two-stage least squares and warns when the instrument is weak (first-stage F below 10). Every method states its assumption; none of them can prove that no confounder is missing.

docs.title: Survival
docs.text: How long until something happens (a customer leaves, a machine fails, a lead buys), counting the cases that have not happened yet. Pick the time column, the column that says whether the event happened (1 or yes, 0 or no) and, optionally, a column to compare groups. You get Kaplan-Meier curves with their confidence bands, the time by which half of each group had the event, and a log-rank test that says whether the groups really differ.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: AutoML picks an algorithm from the size and shape of the data and explains why. You can also choose the algorithm or import a model you trained earlier. Results include metrics, feature importance, a row explanation and a what-if simulator.

docs.title: Model lab
docs.text:
The careful way to choose a model. Pick the target, the columns to leave out and the models to compare; the lab keeps a share of rows aside, scores every model with cross-validation on the rest, tunes the best one with a randomized search, and only then measures it once on the held-out rows. Along the way it:

  • warns about data leaks: columns that predict the target suspiciously well on their own
  • warns about imbalanced classes and can weight rarer classes
  • draws diagnostics: predicted against actual and residuals (regression), confusion matrix, ROC, precision-recall and calibration (classification), and a learning curve
  • explains the model with permutation importance, partial dependence for any feature, and the effect of each feature on one chosen row

The Explain tab adds Shapley values for one row (the contribution of each feature, fairer than replacing one at a time when features are related) and a global importance computed from them. The Errors tab answers "where does the model fail?":

  • segments (a value of a category, a band of a number) where the error is clearly higher than average, with how many times worse and how sure that is
  • the rows it gets most wrong
  • for two-class problems, what each decision threshold gives (precision, recall, F1) and the cheapest threshold for your cost of a false alarm and of a miss
  • a row-by-row comparison of any two models, with a verdict on whether the difference is statistically reliable

Three more tabs look at the trained model from other angles:

  • Uncertainty. A range around each regression prediction, or a short list of plausible classes for each classification row, that holds the truth about as often as you ask (80 to 99%). It is calibrated on half of the test rows and checked on the other half, and it shows the coverage actually observed.
  • What would change it. Pick a test row and the answer you would like (another class, or a value above a number) and the lab searches for the smallest changes to one or two variables that get there, leaving fixed the ones that cannot change (age, country). Useful to explain a decision and to see which levers exist.
  • Fairness. For a classifier, how each group of another column is treated: the rate of the favourable result, the true and false positive rates and the accuracy, with a warning when a group gets the favourable result at less than 80% of another group's rate or when error rates differ by more than 10 points. It cannot say what is fair, only what you would need to justify.

The model list also offers SVM, AdaBoost, Bagging, a voting ensemble and a stacking ensemble (slower, so unticked by default) and, if PyTorch is installed (pip install "kikolens[torch]"), a PyTorch multilayer network that takes part in the same comparison, tuning and model packages.

docs.title: Feature ideas
docs.text: Tries new columns (products, ratios, sums, differences, logarithms of skewed columns, squares) and keeps, one at a time, the ones that improve a model in cross-validation by at least the amount you set. The result is a list of formulas; one click adds them to your data as add_column steps, so they are in the recipe and replay on new data.

docs.title: Feature selection
docs.text: Which columns are worth keeping to predict a target. Four methods score every column (mutual information, an L1-penalised linear model, permutation importance and a random forest) and vote; a cross-validated curve shows the score using the best k columns and the page recommends the smallest k within one standard error of the best. One click adds a recipe step that drops the columns you can leave out.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text: For understanding rather than predicting: what pushes a result up or down, other things equal. A column with numbers gets a linear regression; a column with two values gets a logistic regression. Pick the columns to explain it with and you get each effect with its standard error, its 95% range and its p-value, a coefficient chart, the effect of each term written as a sentence ("each extra unit of size goes with price rising by 3.01, other things equal"; "a support ticket multiplies the odds of leaving by 1.6") and the standardized effect so that terms in different units can be compared. Categories are compared with the commonest value. The page warns about columns that are largely explained by others (unstable coefficients), errors whose spread changes with the fit or that are related from row to row (p-values too optimistic), and, for logistic regression, a column that almost gives the answer away.

docs.title: Neural network
docs.text: A multilayer perceptron you configure: hidden layers (presets or your own, e.g. 128, 64, 32), activation, optimizer, learning rate, L2 regularization, maximum epochs, early stopping and the held-out share for testing. After training you get metrics, the network diagram, the training curve, permutation importance and, if a classical model was trained for the same target, a side-by-side comparison.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
Choose a date column and a numeric column. The page resamples to a regular period, estimates trend and seasonality, and forecasts ahead with a 95% range. The forecast is tested on the last part of the data and compared with repeating the last value; the page says plainly when it does not beat that baseline.

Below the forecast, Go further has three tabs. Compare models tests five models (naive, seasonal naive, trend + seasonality, Holt-Winters and boosting on lags) by training each on the past and forecasting the stretch that follows, several times; the most accurate wins, and the range comes from the real errors it made. You can list special dates (a campaign, a holiday) that the boosting model uses. Changes in the series finds level shifts and trend changes and stays quiet on a series without them. One forecast per group forecasts each region or product separately.

docs.title: Classical series
docs.text: Four tabs on one series (rows of the same period are combined by mean or sum). Stationarity runs ADF (null: unit root) and KPSS (null: stationary) on the series and on its first and second differences and says what the two tests say together: when they agree the verdict is firm, when they disagree the page tells you it is inconclusive and why, and it suggests how many differences to take. Autocorrelation draws the autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation with the band that noise would give and the Ljung-Box test. STL decomposition separates trend, seasonal pattern and remainder, robustly if you ask (outliers then stay in the remainder instead of bending the trend), with the strength of trend and season from 0 to 1 and the unusual points. ARIMA fits a model with seasonal terms, either one you choose or the best of a small search by AICc (listed under "Models tried", with a warning when several are indistinguishable), draws the forecast with its range and checks it against repeating the last season on stretches it did not see; if the simple method wins, the page says so.

docs.title: Forecast with drivers
docs.text: Forecasts a series using other columns too (price, promotions, weather...). It tests on the past whether the drivers really beat the series alone, with a significance test, and lets you try what-if scenarios ("price 10% higher"). The second tab runs a Granger test: does the past of one column help predict another? It is about prediction, not proof of cause.

docs.title: Predict
docs.text:
Use a model on data it has not seen. Choose a model trained in this session, one from your saved models, or open a model file, then:

  • Predict a file. Use the open dataset or upload another file. Before predicting, the page lists problems with the input: missing columns, values that could not be read, categories never seen in training, numbers far outside the training range. Regression gives a likely range for each row; classification gives a confidence, and rows under 60% are counted so you know where to look first. If the file is raw, tick the box to repeat the cleaning steps used for training.
  • Predict one row. A form built from what the model expects, with the training range of each input.
  • Save and share. Keep the model in your saved models (saving the same name again creates a new version), download the package, or download a Markdown model card with its metrics, most influential features and expected inputs.

docs.title: Model health
docs.text: Is a saved model still as good as when you tested it? Choose a model and upload newer data that includes the real results (the column the model predicts). The page scores every period (or five consecutive parts if there is no date), draws the error or accuracy against what the model had in testing, and warns when a period is clearly worse (an average error 1.5 times higher, or an accuracy 10 points lower) or when it keeps getting worse over time. Drift in the inputs is a clue; this is the proof. The Compare models tab scores several saved models on the same data and says which predicts better and whether the gap is reliable or could be chance.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Watches a data source over time. Create a monitor from the data open now (it becomes the baseline), optionally with a saved model and validation rules; then check new data, either a file you upload or the file the monitor watches. Each check records the number of rows, the quality score, drift against the baseline, broken rules and the model's predictions, and raises alerts: drift at the level you chose, a drop in quality, a large change in rows, missing or new columns, columns that changed from numbers to text, model inputs outside what it saw in training, and a shift in the average prediction or in the model's confidence. The history is a chart and a table. KikoLens does not schedule anything itself: the Schedule it panel gives the cron and Windows commands.

docs.title: Run history
docs.text: Every training of the model lab (dashboard or kikolens lab) is recorded with its data, target, parameters and metrics. See them over time with the best so far, sort by any metric, and compare runs side by side (only what differs). The lab can also tune with Bayesian optimisation, which learns from each attempt to choose the next one and shows how the search went.

docs.title: Concept lab
docs.text:
An area of its own ("Learn") for understanding the ideas behind the other sections, with simulations instead of formulas. It needs no data and can be opened from the welcome screen. Pick a concept, move its controls and the simulation redraws; Draw new random data repeats it with another sample so you see what changes (the numbers) and what does not (the lesson). Each concept ends with what to take from it and something to try:

  • The central limit theorem: choose a skewed, two-humped or heavy-tailed population and see the averages of n values turn into a bell as n grows.
  • What a p-value is: with no real effect, about 5 experiments in 100 look significant, and checking the result ten times and stopping at the first success raises that to about 20.
  • What "confidence" means: draw 100 intervals and count the ones that miss the truth; with tiny, skewed samples the promise of 95 % is not kept.
  • How many people are enough: the power curve, the sample needed for the effect you choose (64 per group for half a standard deviation) and why half the effect needs four times the people.
  • Bias, variance and overfitting: polynomials of growing complexity fitted to noisy data, with the error on the data used and on new data split into bias, variance and noise.
  • Simpson's paradox: a trend that goes up in every group and down in the whole data.
  • Regression to the mean: why the best of one year fall back the next with no change in anyone.
  • Why testing many things finds something: twenty tests with nothing real still give a false alarm in two studies out of three, and what two corrections do about it.

docs.title: Glossary and reading guides
docs.text: Glossary (Learn area) lists 74 terms, from p-value to Cpk, each with a plain definition, a "watch out" line with the usual misreading, and related terms. Search matches names first and then definitions, and the language follows the one you chose for the dashboard. At the end of 27 sections (experiments, causal effect, regression, model lab, time series, text, network, survey and others) a closed box called How to read this page says what to look at first, what to be careful about and defines the words that help for that page. The same glossary is available as kikolens glossary and kl.glossary.

docs.title: Panel
docs.text: A page of your own. Add metrics (count, sum, mean, median, minimum, maximum, distinct values), charts (bar, line, area, scatter, histogram, box, pie) and tables, set filters that apply to the whole panel, and reorder or remove tiles. Suggest a panel builds a starting point from your columns. Click a bar or slice, or drag a box on a histogram, scatter or line, and the other tiles filter to what you selected (the chart you clicked keeps showing every option so you can change your mind); the active selections are listed above the tiles and Clear the selections removes them. Download it as one self-contained web page (charts included, the data is not) or as a JSON definition that you can reload and that is saved in your project.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
• Files: CSV, TSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, JSON lines or Feather.
  • Excel workbook: one file with the data, the column profile, statistics, quality issues, the recipe, rule results, model metrics and the last predictions, each on its own sheet, with a highlighted header, frozen first row, filters and sensible widths. Text that starts with = is stored as text, never as a formula.
  • Database: writes the current data as a table. It stops if the table exists unless you choose to add rows or to replace it, and replacing needs a confirmation.

docs.title: Data dictionary and notebook
docs.text: Two more tabs in Export. The data dictionary has one entry per column (meaning, empty share, distinct values, typical values, range, warnings such as "mostly empty" or "may contain personal data") and you write the descriptions in the table itself; download it as Markdown or CSV to hand over with the data. The notebook is a Jupyter file that reloads the data, repeats every recipe step of the session and, if you choose a column, trains a model with the lab; it runs as is.

docs.title: Report
docs.text: Builds one self-contained HTML page with quality, statistics, correlations, patterns, any models trained in this session and, optionally, commentary from the local model. It also builds a PDF (cover, quality, distributions, correlations and, when available, the model and the autopilot's forecast) that you can download directly.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
• Save. Packs the original data, the recipe, extra datasets, your notes and, if you tick it, the trained models, into one .kikolens file.
  • Open. Restores all of that and replays the recipe, so you land exactly where you stopped. Data are stored as Parquet and never run code; models inside are loaded only when you confirm you trust the file.
  • Recipe. Every cleaning and transformation step, downloadable as JSON or as a Python script. Upload a recipe and a new file with the same columns to get it processed the same way.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
For columns with sentences, such as comments or reviews. Everything runs on this computer.

  • Terms: the words, pairs or triples that appear in the most texts, with a search box that shows each match in context.
  • By group: the terms that distinguish each group of another column (log odds), and the terms that go with a higher or lower number such as a rating.
  • Themes: groups similar texts and describes each by its key terms and an example.
  • Classify: learns to predict a column (a rating, a topic) from the text, tells you whether it beats always guessing the commonest class, shows the terms that point to each class and lets you try a sentence.
  • Tone: a rough positive / negative picture from a small word list (English and Spanish). It does not understand irony or negation.
  • Summary: asks the local model (Ollama) for the main themes of a sample of the texts.

Topics finds the themes in the texts with NMF (fast and steady) or LDA, tries 2 to 8 topics and keeps the one whose main words co-occur most (coherence; the table shows the others), lists each topic's main words, its share of the texts and three example texts, and warns when two topics share most of their words or when most texts mix several topics. Pick a date column to see each topic's share by month. Duplicates and similar groups near-identical texts (typos and small edits included) and finds the texts most like a phrase you type. Patterns lists emails, links, phones, amounts, percentages, dates, hashtags and mentions; they are patterns, not understanding, and personal data found is flagged for the Privacy section. Phrases shows key phrases (RAKE) and word pairs that appear together more than chance. Readability gives a reading-ease score per text.

docs.title: Customers
docs.text:
Four tabs for behaviour data.

  • Retention. Cohorts by the period of each customer's first activity, and the share of each cohort still active one, two, three periods later. Periods that have not happened yet are left blank, not shown as zero.
  • Segments (RFM). Recency, frequency and spend scored from 1 to 5 and turned into segments (champions, loyal, big spenders, new or promising, at risk, lost), with the share of the value each one holds. Download every customer with their segment.
  • Funnel. Choose the stages in order; users count at a stage only if they also reached the earlier ones, and the biggest drop is named.
  • Bought together. Association rules (Apriori) from an order column and an item column, with support, confidence and lift.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: Did a change move the numbers? Before and after a date compares what happened after the change with what the earlier trend (or, much better, control series that the change did not touch) predicted. The range comes from how wrong the same method was at predicting earlier stretches where nothing happened, so it is not overconfident. Treated and control groups is a difference-in-differences estimate with a confidence interval. Neither proves causation: they only count as the effect of the change if nothing else changed at the same time.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text: From a table of who used or rated what, an item-based recommender suggests items to a person, lists the items most like another, and is evaluated honestly: one interaction of each person is hidden and the recommender must bring it back among its first suggestions, against simply recommending the most popular items.

docs.title: Survey
docs.text: Seven tabs for questionnaire data (one row per respondent). Questions summarises the scale questions (numbers such as 1 to 5, or texts such as "Agree" and "Strongly agree", in English or Spanish): average, share favourable, neutral and unfavourable, and the spread of answers; questions worded the other way round can be reversed. Reliability gives Cronbach's alpha for a group of questions that measure the same thing, its 95 % range, how well each question moves with the rest and what alpha would be without it, and points at questions that look reversed. NPS computes promoters minus detractors with its range and, by group, which groups stand out from the rest. Cross-tab crosses two questions with the chi-square test, Cramér's V and residuals that show which cells have more or fewer answers than chance. What matters most uses relative weights to share the explained part of an overall rating between the questions that may drive it, even when they overlap, and crosses importance with score: important and low-scoring means improve first. Between groups finds the questions that score differently, using tests for ordered answers and a correction for the number of questions. Answer quality counts people who gave the same answer to everything, left most blank or answered too fast.

docs.title: Network
docs.text: Choose the two columns that name the ends of each link (customer and product, sender and receiver, author and paper), optionally a column with the strength of each link, and whether links have a direction. Overview lists the nodes by importance (PageRank, number of connections, betweenness: how many shortest paths pass through the node, and clustering: how many of its neighbours know each other), the communities found, how much of the network is in one connected piece, the typical and longest distance, and a drawing of the most important nodes coloured by community. Notes say when the network is split, depends on a few hubs or has bridges: nodes with few links that hold parts together. Paths finds the shortest chain between two nodes. Missing links suggests pairs that are not linked but share many neighbours. Robustness removes the best-connected nodes step by step and shows how fast the largest piece shrinks compared with removing random nodes.

docs.title: Geography
docs.text: Pick the latitude and longitude columns (they are found by name and range). Check and map counts the usable rows and warns about swapped columns, values out of range, missing coordinates and the 0, 0 point that GPS devices report without a signal, and draws the points on a globe with no map tiles; coastlines and countries are optional because Plotly downloads those shapes. Distances gives the kilometres to a place or to the nearest centre in a CSV of shops or warehouses, and how many points each centre serves. Zones finds dense groups of points, optionally averaging a column in each. Spatial pattern asks whether nearby places have similar values (Moran's I, with a permutation p-value) and marks hot and cold spots (Getis-Ord Gi), corrected for the many places tested at once. Grid* summarises points in square cells of the size you choose. Distances are along the surface of a sphere, which is accurate enough for business decisions but not for surveying.

docs.title: Model governance
docs.text: Three tabs. Overview lists every registered model with its stage, owner, risk, latest validation and whether a review is due, and warns when a model file no longer matches what was registered. Model takes a saved model through its life: register it with an owner, a risk level and a card (purpose, intended use, limitations); validate it on the open data, which must contain the real results (the page says whether it holds up and gives the range the result could fall in); see, for the stage you choose, which checks pass and which do not, and move it; approve it (for high risk, by someone other than the owner); and roll production back. Overriding a failed check needs a reason and is logged as an override. Audit log verifies the chain of hashes and lists every action. The name you type as "who is doing this" is recorded as typed: the log is a record for the team, not access control.

docs.title: Synthetic data
docs.text: Generates a table that looks like yours (each column with its distribution, and the columns with the same correlations) but whose rows are not real people, with a report on fidelity (how close the distributions and correlations are), privacy (exact and near copies of real rows) and utility (a model trained on the synthetic data against one trained on the real data, both tested on real rows).

docs.title: Development
docs.text: The short version is in CONTRIBUTING.md. This page explains how the checks are organised.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every pull request into develop or main runs:

Job What it checks Lint ruff check for unused imports and variables, undefined names and syntax errors. Tests The whole suite on Linux with Python 3.12 and the latest pandas, with coverage. Compatibility The suite on Linux with pandas 2, on Windows with pandas 3, and, as warnings that do not block, on macOS and with Python 3.13. Build package Builds the wheel, installs it and runs the command line, including kikolens doctor. Documentation mkdocs build --strict: a broken link or a missing page fails the build. CodeQL Security analysis of the Python code, also weekly. SonarCloud Code quality, from the coverage of the Tests job.

Dependabot proposes monthly updates of the dependencies and the actions into develop.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
1. Move the Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md under the new version and set __version__ in kikolens/__init__.py and version in pyproject.toml.
  2. Merge develop into main with a pull request.
  3. Push the tag, for example git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "1.0.0" && git push origin v1.0.0.

The Release workflow checks that the tag matches the package version, builds the wheel and the source archive, and creates the GitHub release with the changelog notes of that version. Publishing to PyPI is deliberately manual, because it cannot be undone.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• tests/test_dashboard.py and the other AppTest based tests drive the real Streamlit script headlessly.
  • tests/conftest.py points KIKOLENS_HOME at a temporary folder so no test writes to a real user folder.
  • Tests of the analyses plant a known effect (a coefficient, a changed region, a drifted period) and check that it is found, and plant none and check that it is not.

docs.title: Docs and screenshots
docs.text:
pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve                       # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
pip install -e ".[docs]" && python -m playwright install chromium
python docs/make_screenshots.py    # regenerates the example data and every image (about 25 minutes)

docs.title: Preparing the data
docs.text:
The classical models, the neural network and the lab share the same ideas:

  1. Rows with a missing target are dropped.
  2. Date columns become three numbers: days since 1970, month and weekday.
  3. Text columns are one-hot encoded; in AutoML and the neural network those with 50 or more distinct values are dropped, in the lab up to 30 categories are kept per column (rarer ones are grouped), columns with a different value in every row are dropped as identifiers, and so are text columns with more distinct values than half the rows.
  4. Missing numbers are filled with the median, then everything is standardized.

The target is a regression target when it is numeric with more than 20 distinct values, and a classification target otherwise. A date target, or a classification target with more than 50 classes, is rejected with an explanation.

Twenty percent of the rows are held out; every reported metric is measured on them.

docs.title: AutoML
docs.text: In automatic mode the choice depends on the data: ridge regression for small regression problems, lasso when there are many columns for the rows available, random forest otherwise; logistic regression for small classification problems and gradient boosting for larger ones. The page shows the rationale. You can override it with random forest, gradient boosting, decision tree, ridge/logistic or lasso/KNN.

docs.title: Model lab
docs.text:
The lab exists to answer "which model should I trust?" without fooling yourself.

  1. Split first. A share of the rows (20% by default) is set aside and not touched until the very end.
  2. Preprocessing lives inside each model. Imputers, scalers and encoders are fitted only on the training part of each cross-validation fold, so nothing from the validation rows leaks into training.
  3. Compare. Every selected model is scored with k-fold cross-validation (stratified for classification). A baseline (predict the mean, or the most common class) is always in the table: a model that does not beat it has learned nothing.
  4. Tune the best. A randomized search over sensible ranges. The tuned version replaces the default only if it scores better in cross-validation.
  5. Test once. The chosen model is scored on the held-out rows. Those are the numbers to report.
  6. Check for problems.
  7. Leakage: a numeric column whose rank correlation with the target is 0.98 or more is flagged, and so is any column that, on its own and with a shallow decision tree, predicts the target almost perfectly (cross-validated score of 0.98 or more, and clearly better than the baseline). Such columns are often a copy of the answer or something only known afterwards.
  8. Imbalance: when the rarest class is under 10% of the rows accuracy becomes misleading, so the lab recommends balanced accuracy or F1 and offers class weighting.
  9. Learning curve: shows whether more data would help.

The default list is twelve models. Five more are available on request: an SVM (with the target scaled for regression), AdaBoost, Bagging, a voting ensemble (random forest, histogram gradient boosting and a linear model, averaging predictions or probabilities) and a stacking ensemble (the same three, combined by a linear model trained on their cross-validated predictions). If PyTorch is installed, a PyTorch MLP joins them: Adam, dropout, weight decay and early stopping on 15% of the training rows, with the same preprocessing as every other model.

Primary metrics: R-squared for regression, weighted F1 for classification. Regression also reports RMSE and MAE; classification adds accuracy, balanced accuracy, ROC AUC and, for two classes, the Brier score.

Importance is measured by permutation on the held-out rows. Partial dependence shows the average prediction as one feature changes. The per-row explanation replaces one feature at a time with a typical value and reports how much the prediction moves.

docs.title: Uncertainty (conformal prediction)
docs.text: Split conformal prediction. Half of the held-out test rows calibrate: for regression the score of a row is the absolute error, for classification one minus the probability given to the true class. The threshold is the ceil((n + 1) * coverage) / n quantile of those scores, and it gives a range prediction ± threshold or the set of classes whose probability is at least 1 - threshold. The guarantee, that new rows fall inside about coverage of the time, holds without assuming normal errors but only if new data resemble the calibration rows. The other half of the test rows measures the coverage actually obtained.

docs.title: Counterfactuals
docs.text: For one row, the search tries every value of one variable (15 quantiles of a number, up to 30 categories), then pairs of the six most influential variables, and keeps the changes that give the wanted answer. They are ranked by how many variables change and then by the total standardised distance. Variables you mark as fixed never move.
