The result says what the model would do, not what would happen in the world.

docs.title: Fairness
docs.text: For each group of a column: the share of rows that receive the favourable prediction (selection rate), the true positive rate, the false positive rate and the accuracy. The warnings use the four-fifths guideline (the lowest selection rate divided by the highest, below 0.8) and gaps of more than 10 points in the true or false positive rate. Groups under 10 rows are left out.

docs.title: Feature search
docs.text: Candidates are built from up to eight numeric columns: a logarithm (log1p, for non-negative skewed columns), a square, and the product, the two ratios, the sum and the difference of every pair. The 24 most rank-correlated with the target are scored by cross-validated histogram gradient boosting, and added greedily while each improves the score by at least the chosen threshold. Because the evaluation is cross-validated and the formulas are applied with the safe expression interpreter, the gain is not an artefact of the training rows and the result replays on new data.

docs.title: Survival
docs.text: The Kaplan-Meier estimate multiplies, at each event time, the share of those still at risk that did not have the event; the band is the log-log Greenwood interval. The log-rank test compares observed with expected events in each group at every event time, using the hypergeometric variance. It assumes that censoring is unrelated to the outcome.

docs.title: Distribution fit
docs.text: Each candidate is fitted by maximum likelihood with SciPy (the location is fixed at zero for distributions defined on positive values) and scored with AIC, 2k - 2 log L, where k counts the fitted parameters; the lowest is best and a difference under 2 is a tie. A distribution is tried only if the data can belong to it: positive values for lognormal, gamma and Weibull, non-negative for exponential, between 0 and 1 for beta. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test uses parameters estimated from the same data, which makes its p-value too generous, so it is shown as a guide. Normality uses Shapiro-Wilk on up to 5,000 values.

docs.title: Bayesian optimisation
docs.text: A Gaussian process (Matern 5/2 kernel plus noise) is fitted to the cross-validated scores seen so far, over the search space mapped to the unit cube (log scale for parameters such as a learning rate, integer and categorical parameters handled). The next combination is the one with the highest expected improvement among 2,000 random candidates. A quarter of the attempts (at least 3) are random exploration first. A combination that fails is recorded as such and the search goes on.

docs.title: Sequential tests
docs.text: The mSPRT mixes the likelihood ratio over a normal prior for the effect, N(0, tau^2): Lambda_n = sqrt(s2 / (s2 + n tau^2)) * exp(n^2 tau^2 D^2 / (2 s2 (s2 + n tau^2))), where D is the running mean of the pairwise differences and s2 their variance. It is a martingale under no effect, so by Ville's inequality P(Lambda ever >= 1/alpha) <= alpha however often it is checked; the test stops when it crosses 1/alpha. The always-valid p-value is min(1, 1 / max Lambda), and the interval is the set of effects the same test would not reject. tau defaults to 20% of the standard deviation of the differences; validity does not depend on it, only how fast it detects. Observations are paired in arrival order, the k-th of each group. An effect estimated at the moment of stopping tends to be exaggerated, as with any early stop. The bandit is Thompson sampling with Beta posteriors, allocating visitors in batches.

docs.title: Forecast with drivers and Granger tests
docs.text: The Granger F-test compares a regression of the effect on its own past with one that adds the past of the cause, for every lag from 1 to the maximum, with a Bonferroni correction because several lags are tried; by default it works on first differences so that a trend shared by both columns is not mistaken for a relation. The forecast uses gradient boosting on lags of the target and of the drivers (plus day of week and month); it is tested with four rolling-origin folds of one-step-ahead predictions, with and without the drivers, and a Wilcoxon test on the paired absolute errors decides whether they help. Future values of the drivers are assumed equal to their last observed value, or to the scenario factors you give.

docs.title: Feature selection
docs.text: Mutual information uses the original columns (categories as codes). The L1 model is a Lasso (or an L1 logistic regression) on the standardised preprocessed matrix, with each column's coefficients added across its indicator columns. Permutation importance comes from a histogram gradient boosting on a held-out 30%; the random forest uses its impurity importances. Ranks are averaged. The score of the best k columns is cross-validated with the same booster, and the recommended k is the smallest whose mean score is within one standard error of the best.

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text: The Gaussian mixture is fitted for 1 to k_max components (full covariances if there are at least 20 rows per column, otherwise diagonal) and the lowest BIC wins; a row's confidence is its highest membership probability. The hierarchical method uses SciPy linkage and cuts the tree into the requested number of groups (above 2,500 rows it groups a sample and assigns the rest to the nearest group centre). DBSCAN's radius is where the sorted distance to the 5th neighbour bends most (largest second difference of the smoothed curve). Each group is described by the two columns whose group mean is furthest from the overall mean in standard deviations (shown only if beyond 0.4).

docs.title: Recommender
docs.text: Item-item cosine similarity on the person-by-item matrix, multiplied by common / (common + shrinkage) so that pairs sharing few people count less. A person's score for an item is the sum of its similarity to the items they have used; seen items are excluded and unknown people get the most popular items. Evaluation hides one interaction for each person with at least three, refits without it and counts how often the hidden item is in the top k, against the top k most popular items the person has not used.

docs.title: Synthetic data
docs.text: A Gaussian copula. Each column becomes normal scores through its ranks (a category occupies a probability interval and a point inside it is drawn); the correlation matrix of the scores is repaired to be positive semi-definite and a multivariate normal is sampled; each coordinate goes back through the column's empirical quantiles (numbers and dates) or its category frequencies. Identifiers are regenerated, long free text is skipped, and each column's share of empty values is reproduced independently. The report gives, per column, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance (numbers) or total variation distance (categories); the mean gap between Spearman correlations; the share of synthetic rows that exactly equal a real row; the share closer to a real row than a fifth of the usual distance between two real rows; and the train-on-synthetic, test-on-real utility. Relations that are not captured by pairwise correlation (for example an interaction of three columns) are not reproduced.

docs.title: The analyst
docs.text:
The language model never writes or runs code. Three pieces keep that true.

  • A client (kikolens/ai/client.py) that talks to Ollama and asks for JSON. The answer is extracted from whatever text surrounds it and passed through a validator; if the validator raises, its message is appended to the prompt and the model tries again (twice by default). After that the error is shown to the user.
  • A chart specification (kikolens/ai/chartspec.py): kind (bar, line, area, scatter, histogram, box, pie, heatmap), columns, aggregation, time grain, filters and top N. Every column is checked against the data (case-insensitively), every filter value is coerced to the column's type, and an impossible chart (a sum of a text column, filters that leave no rows) is refused with the valid options listed. The chart is drawn by KikoLens' own functions.
  • A tool registry (kikolens/ai/analyst.py) with thirteen tools, each with typed arguments (a column, a list of columns, a number, one of a few words). A call is accepted only if the tool exists, the arguments are the ones it takes and every column is real. A tool that fails is recorded and the loop continues; repeating a call ends the loop; at most five steps run. The final answer is written from the short summaries of the steps, not from raw rows, and the steps can be exported as the equivalent calls of the Python API.

Prompts contain the column names, types, ranges, and, unless switched off, up to eight values of each categorical column and nothing else; no row of data is sent (text classification is the exception, since reading the texts is the job). Everything stays on this computer because the model does.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Detection samples up to 2,000 values per column and flags it when at least 60% pass the check for a pattern. The checks are not just shapes: card numbers must pass the Luhn algorithm, IBANs the mod-97 check, and Spanish DNI/NIE numbers must carry the right letter, so ordinary long numbers are not reported. Columns named like personal data (name, email, phone, birth...) are flagged by name, with the reason shown. Masking keeps the last characters; fingerprints are SHA-256(salt + value) cut to 12 hex characters by default. A salted fingerprint cannot be reversed, but anyone who has the salt can test whether a known value is present, which is why the recipe that holds it should stay private. k-anonymity groups the rows by the combination of descriptive columns and reports the size of each group; rows in a group of one are unique and the easiest to re-identify.

docs.title: Matching records
docs.text: Names are lowercased, stripped of accents and punctuation and their words sorted, so "García, Ana" and "ana garcia" are equal. Candidates for each row are the rows of the other table that share a rare word (a word in more than 20% of the rows is ignored); an exact match short-circuits the search. Each candidate gets the larger of the character similarity (Ratcliff-Obershelp) and a blend of it with the share of words in common. The best partner above the threshold is kept, and a match is marked ambiguous when the runner-up scores within 0.03 of it.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text: Linear regression is solved by least squares; the standard errors are the classical ones, sigma^2 (X'X)^-1, with t intervals and p-values on the residual degrees of freedom. Categories become indicators with the commonest value as the reference; dates become days since the first. The page reports R-squared and adjusted R-squared, the F test of the whole model, the variance inflation factor of each term, the Durbin-Watson statistic (about 2 when neighbouring errors are unrelated), a Breusch-Pagan test (regressing the squared errors on the terms; a small p-value means their spread changes with the fit) and a Shapiro-Wilk test of the errors. Logistic regression is fitted by Newton-Raphson on standardized columns, so the Wald intervals and p-values come from the inverse information matrix; coefficients are also shown as odds ratios, with McFadden's pseudo R-squared, the likelihood-ratio test, AUC and the accuracy against always guessing the commonest. Rows with an empty value in any used column are left out and counted.

docs.title: Model health
docs.text: The model scores the rows whose real result is known and the errors are grouped by period. For a number the reference is the mean absolute error measured on the held-out rows when the model was built, and a period is flagged when its error is at least 1.5 times that; for a category it is the accuracy, flagged when 10 points lower. Periods with fewer than 20 rows are reported but not judged. A trend warning appears when the rank correlation (Spearman) between time and the metric of the judged periods is significant (p below 0.05) in the direction of getting worse, with at least four periods.

docs.title: Unusual periods in a series
docs.text: The expected value of each period is a centred rolling median (the trend) plus the median of what is left at each position of the cycle (the seasonal pattern, with the period guessed from the autocorrelation). The residual is scaled with the median absolute deviation, which a few spikes cannot inflate, and a period is flagged when the scaled value is beyond the sensitivity (3.5 by default). min_gap merges runs of neighbouring flags into one.

docs.title: Comparing saved models
docs.text: Both models score the same rows. For a number, the absolute errors of the two are compared with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test; for a category, the rows where only one is right are compared with an exact binomial test (the McNemar idea). The first model by mean absolute error (or weighted F1) is the champion, and the page says whether its lead is reliable at the 5% level or could be chance.

docs.title: Why it changed
docs.text: Two periods are compared. For a total or a count, each value of a column contributes the difference of its own total, so the contributions add up to the change exactly. For an average, the change is sum over values of (w_after - w_before) * (m_before - M_before) (mix: the value weighs more or less) plus sum of w_after * (m_after - m_before) (rate: its average moved), where w is the share of rows and m the average of the value; the two add up to the change exactly. A value that exists in only one period has all its effect in the mix. Columns are ranked by the share of the total absolute contribution held by their single biggest value.

docs.title: Customers
docs.text: Retention: a cohort is the period of a user's first activity, and the cell for age a is the share of that cohort active in period cohort + a; ages beyond the last observed period are blank. RFM: recency (days since the last activity), frequency and total spend are ranked into five equal groups; the segments are rules over the three scores. Funnel: a user is counted at a stage only if they appear at it and at every earlier one. Association rules: Apriori finds the sets of items present in at least support of the baskets; for each, confidence is P(right | left) and lift is confidence / P(right).

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: Before and after a date: the expected series is a ridge regression of the measure on the control series fitted before the change, or, without controls, the best forecast model of the earlier trend. The uncertainty is taken from the error the same method made on earlier windows of the same length, where nothing happened, and widened with a t distribution because there are few such windows. Difference in differences: the coefficient of treated × after in a linear regression of the outcome, with its t interval; it assumes both groups would have moved alike without the treatment.

docs.title: Bayesian A/B
docs.text: Rates use a Beta posterior (uniform prior unless set). Averages use the t distribution of the mean of each group. The probability that the variant is better is the share of 200,000 draws where it beats the control, and the expected loss is the average shortfall when the choice is wrong.

docs.title: Neural network
docs.text:
A multilayer perceptron from scikit-learn (MLPRegressor or MLPClassifier).

  • Regression targets are standardized inside the model and predictions come back in the original units. Without this a network cannot learn a target such as revenue in the thousands.
  • Early stopping holds out 10% of the training rows and stops when the validation score stops improving. It is unavailable with the lbfgs optimizer.
  • Importance is measured by permutation: shuffle one column on the test rows and see how much the score drops. This works for any model.
  • The architecture chart draws at most 12 nodes per layer; the legend shows the real size.

Rules of thumb: start with the Medium preset; if training and validation curves diverge, raise the L2 regularization or shrink the network; if both are poor, give it more epochs or a larger network. Networks need at least 20 rows and usually beat classical models only on larger, non-linear data.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
1. The date column is parsed, sorted and aggregated to a regular period (mean by default). Gaps are interpolated.
  2. Decomposition splits the series into trend (centered moving average), a repeating seasonal pattern and a remainder. The seasonal period comes from the frequency (7 for daily, 12 for monthly, and so on) or, failing that, from the autocorrelation.
  3. Forecast fits a linear trend plus Fourier terms for the seasonality. The range shown is 95% and widens with distance.
  4. Backtest. The last stretch of the data is hidden, forecast, and compared with the truth and with a naive baseline that repeats the last value. If the model does not beat the baseline the dashboard warns you.

This is a deliberately simple model. It handles trend and one seasonal cycle well; it does not know about holidays, promotions or sudden changes.

docs.title: Forecasting models
docs.text:
Five models share one interface, and each can be tested on its own:

  • Naive repeats the last value; seasonal naive repeats the last full cycle.
  • Trend + seasonality is the linear trend plus Fourier terms described above.
  • Holt-Winters is the additive version with a damped trend: a level, a trend and one seasonal profile, updated at each step; its smoothing parameters are found by minimizing the one-step squared error. With fewer than two cycles of data it drops the seasonality.
  • Lag boosting removes a linear trend, then fits a gradient-boosting model on the previous values (1, 2, 3, 7, 14 and one season back), a rolling mean and deviation, the weekday, month, day of year and a flag for the special dates you give. It forecasts recursively, feeding its own predictions back as lags.

Choosing. The series is cut at several points (up to three); at each, every model is trained on what came before and forecasts the next stretch (as long as the horizon, up to a quarter of the series). The model with the lowest mean absolute error wins, and the table also gives RMSE and MASE (error relative to repeating the previous value). The final model is refitted on all the data. Range. The interval is not a formula: it is the 5th to 95th percentile of the real errors the winning model made at each step ahead in those tests, and it cannot narrow as the horizon grows. With few test points it borrows from all steps. Changes. The series is split recursively where fitting two straight lines instead of one reduces the squared error by more than a penalty proportional to the noise (estimated from second differences) times the logarithm of the length, so noise alone produces no change points. A change is a level shift when the jump exceeds three times the noise and a trend change otherwise.

docs.title: Statistical tests
docs.text:
Every test returns the p-value, an effect size and a sentence. A small p-value says a difference is unlikely to be chance; the effect size says whether it is big enough to matter, and with lots of rows even trivial differences become "significant".

Question Test chosen Effect size Do 2 groups differ in a number? Welch's t-test if the groups look normal (or have 30+ rows), otherwise Mann-Whitney U Cohen's d, or rank-biserial r Do 3+ groups differ? One-way ANOVA with Tukey comparisons if normal with similar spread, otherwise Kruskal-Wallis with Holm-adjusted pairwise Mann-Whitney eta squared, or epsilon squared Are two categories related? Chi-squared; Fisher's exact for 2x2 tables with small expected counts Cramér's V Are two numbers correlated? Pearson, with a Fisher-z confidence interval, next to Spearman r Did the treatment change a rate? Two-proportion z-test, 95% interval for the difference, and the probability that the treatment is better from Beta posteriors absolute and relative lift Did it change an average? Welch's t-test difference and lift

Normality is checked with Shapiro-Wilk on small groups; equal spread with Levene. The thresholds for the effect labels follow common conventions (for example Cohen's d: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).

Sample size. For rates, the number of rows per group is (z_a * sqrt(2 p̄ (1 - p̄)) + z_b * sqrt(p1 (1 - p1) + p2 (1 - p2)))^2 / (p2 - p1)^2 at 5% significance and the power you choose; for averages it is 2 ((z_a + z_b) * sd / delta)^2.

Screening many columns. Testing 50 columns at the 5% level produces about two false hits by chance. The screen therefore reports Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values and marks a column as related only if the adjusted value is below the threshold. Each column is compared with the target using the test that fits the two types (Spearman, Kruskal-Wallis or chi-squared), and numbers with 10 or fewer distinct values are treated as categories.

docs.title: Missing data, spellings and rules
docs.text:
• Are gaps random? For each column with gaps, KikoLens tests whether the other columns differ between the rows where it is empty and the rows where it is present (Mann-Whitney for numbers, chi-squared for categories). A gap is called dependent when the best p-value is below 0.001 and the effect is at least 0.2.
  • Smart fill. KNN uses the 5 nearest rows (distance-weighted) on standardized numeric columns. Iterative uses Bayesian ridge regression, cycling over the columns. Both work on numbers only and round columns that hold whole numbers. By group takes the median (or most common value) within each group, falling back to the overall value.
  • Similar spellings. Values are reduced to a key (lowercase, without accents or punctuation); keys are then merged when their similarity ratio is at least the threshold (0.85 by default), and every variant becomes the most frequent form. A change of two letters in a short word is below 0.85: lower the threshold to catch it.
  • Near-duplicates. Each row becomes text; rows are compared with character 2 to 4-grams (TF-IDF, cosine similarity), looking at each row's nearest neighbours. Identical rows are excluded (they are ordinary duplicates).
  • Rules are evaluated per row. Empty values break only the not empty rule. A pattern must match the whole value.

docs.title: Anomalies
docs.text:
Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor and Mahalanobis distance first scale the numeric columns with the median and interquartile range; empty values are filled with the median. The share you choose is the share of rows flagged (the most unusual ones).

  • Isolation Forest isolates rows with random splits; unusual rows need fewer splits.
  • Local Outlier Factor compares the density around a row with that of its neighbours.
  • Robust z-score takes the largest distance from the median, in units of the median absolute deviation, over the columns.
  • Mahalanobis distance measures distance from the centre while accounting for correlations between columns.

For every flagged row, the explanation lists up to three columns whose robust z-score is at least 2.

docs.title: Text
docs.text: Words are lowercase sequences of letters (at least two), with stop words removed (English and Spanish; the language is detected by counting stop words). Terms counts in how many texts each term appears, next to its mean TF-IDF weight. By group ranks terms by the smoothed log odds of being in the group versus elsewhere. Themes uses TF-IDF vectors (reduced with a truncated SVD only when there are more than 400 terms), normalizes them and runs k-means; each theme shows its centroid's top terms and the text closest to its centre. The classifier is TF-IDF on words and pairs of words with a class-balanced logistic regression, scored with cross-validated predictions against the baseline of always predicting the commonest class. Tone counts words from a small positive and negative list. The summary sends a random sample of at most 40 texts, each cut to 400 characters, to the model running in Ollama.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: PCA runs on standardized columns; components for 90% is the smallest number whose cumulative explained variation reaches 90%. t-SNE keeps neighbours close but distorts global distances, so use it to spot groups, not to measure separation. The VIF of a column is 1 / (1 - R²) of regressing it on the others, computed from the inverse of the correlation matrix.

docs.title: Comparing datasets
docs.text: Numeric columns are cut at the deciles of the reference; categorical ones use their categories. The PSI is the sum over bins of (current share - reference share) * ln(current share / reference share). Below 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate and above 0.25 a clear shift. Numbers with 12 or fewer distinct values are compared as categories. Text that holds numbers or dates is converted first, and dates and columns that are different in almost every row (identifiers) are listed as information rather than judged. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (numbers) or chi-squared test (categories) is shown beside the PSI, and a change of 10 points or more in the share of empty values downgrades a stable column to moderate. With large samples the tests flag tiny changes, which is why the verdict uses the PSI.

docs.title: Explaining a model
docs.text:
• Shapley values. For one row, KikoLens draws many random orders of the features. In each order it starts from a random training row and swaps in the features of the row being explained one at a time, recording how much the prediction moves at each step. The average move per feature is its Shapley value; together with the starting value they add up to the prediction exactly. For classifiers the value is in probability of the class you choose. The global version averages the absolute values over a sample of test rows. The cost grows with the number of features, so it is limited to 40.
  • Error analysis. The error is the absolute error (regression) or whether the prediction was wrong (classification). Each category, and each quartile of a number, is compared with the overall error; a segment is reported only if it has at least 8 rows, its error is more than 15% above average and the gap is at least two standard errors, so noise does not produce stories.
  • Threshold and costs. For a two-class model the probability threshold is swept from 0.05 to 0.95. The cost is false alarms × cost of a false alarm + misses × cost of a miss; the cheapest threshold is usually not 0.5 when one mistake costs more than the other.
  • Comparing two models. Both are trained on the same rows and tested on the same held-out rows. For regression the absolute errors are compared with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test; for classification, the rows only one of them gets right are compared with a binomial (McNemar-style) test.

docs.title: Causal inference
docs.text: The effect page estimates the average effect with regression adjustment, inverse-propensity weighting, nearest-neighbour matching on the propensity (average effect on the treated) and an augmented inverse-propensity (doubly robust) estimator, which stays consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome models are right. Propensities and outcome models are cross-fitted (five folds) so overfitting does not leak into the estimate, and propensities are trimmed. Ranges come from a bootstrap, except for the doubly robust estimator, which uses its influence function. Covariate balance is the standardised mean difference before and after weighting, and the E-value follows VanderWeele and Ding. Uplift uses a T-learner with cross-fitting, evaluated with the Qini curve. Discontinuity fits a local polynomial on each side with a triangular kernel and a rule-of-thumb bandwidth, and tests the density around the cutoff with a binomial test. Synthetic control finds non-negative weights summing to one that match the pre-intervention path, and its p-value is the share of placebo units whose post/pre fit ratio is at least as large. Instrumental variables use two-stage least squares with heteroskedasticity-robust errors.

docs.title: Classical time series
docs.text:
ADF regresses the first difference on the lagged level, a constant (and trend) and lagged differences, with the number of lags chosen by AIC; its p-value uses MacKinnon's approximation, checked against the published 1 %, 5 % and 10 % critical values. KPSS uses the partial sums of the residuals over a Newey-West long-run variance and interpolates its p-value in the published table (so it is bounded between 0.01 and 0.10). Both are simulated in the test suite to hold their size and have power. STL follows Cleveland et al.: the seasonal subseries are smoothed by local linear regression, a low-pass filter removes what leaks into the season, the trend is smoothed, and optional bisquare robustness weights are recomputed over several outer rounds; strengths are 1 - var(remainder) / var(component + remainder) on a remainder clipped at four robust standard deviations, so one outlier does not dilute them.

ARIMA models phi(B) Phi(B^m) (1 - B)^d (1 - B^m)^D y = theta(B) Theta(B^m) e with the polynomials multiplied out and the residuals computed by a linear filter. Parameters are found by conditional least squares (the first residuals, which depend on values before the sample, are left out), with stationarity and invertibility guaranteed by a partial-autocorrelation parametrisation; this is close to but not the same as exact maximum likelihood, and very short series or roots near the unit circle show the difference. Forecast ranges use the psi weights of the model and assume normal errors. The automatic search takes the differences from KPSS (and the seasonal difference from the strength of the season), tries p, q up to 3 with p + q <= 4 and P, Q in {0, 1}, and compares AICc on one common sample, because candidates with more autoregressive terms would otherwise drop more initial residuals and look better for free.

docs.title: Model governance
docs.text: Records live in ~/.kikolens/governance (one JSON per model, plus audit.jsonl) and refer to the model by its file name in the registry. At registration the SHA-256 of the model file is stored; promotion and stage references (sales@production) refuse a file whose hash has changed, because it is no longer the model that was documented and validated. A validation scores the model on rows with known results with the same metrics as the model lab and compares one of them (MAE, RMSE, R2 or accuracy) with the training value; because both numbers are noisy, the validation fails only if even the optimistic end of a bootstrap 95 % range of the new metric is worse than the tolerated fraction (20 % by default). The comparison with the production model uses the champion and challenger test of kikolens models compare and blocks only a challenger that is reliably worse. Each audit entry stores the hash of the previous one together with its own content, so changing, removing or inserting a line breaks every hash after it; this reveals tampering to anyone who verifies, but cannot prevent someone with write access to the folder from rewriting the whole log.

docs.title: Text mining
docs.text: Topics use TF-IDF with NMF (or counts with LDA) over words that appear in at least two texts and in at most 60 % of them. Coherence is the UMass measure: for each topic's ten leading words, the mean of log((D(a, b) + 1) / D(b)) over pairs, where D counts the texts containing the word(s); it is a guide rather than a verdict, and the automatic choice often lands on a coarser split than a person would. Near duplicates compare TF-IDF vectors of 3 to 4 letter fragments by cosine similarity, in blocks so that 20,000 texts stay manageable, and join texts above the threshold transitively. RAKE splits texts at stop words and punctuation and scores each word by its degree over its frequency. Collocations are ranked by normalised pointwise mutual information. Readability counts syllables from vowel groups, so scores are approximate. Pattern extraction uses regular expressions for common formats.

docs.title: Network analysis
docs.text: Links are summed into a sparse adjacency matrix (repeated links add their weights; self-loops and rows with a missing end are ignored and reported). PageRank is a power iteration with damping 0.85 that spreads dangling nodes evenly. Betweenness is Brandes' algorithm over hops, exact up to a work budget and otherwise estimated from a random sample of starting nodes and rescaled. Communities come from Louvain modularity optimisation, relabelled from largest to smallest; weak modularity (below 0.3) is flagged. Distances are measured inside the largest connected piece from up to 60 starting nodes, and the longest distance is a double-sweep lower bound. Suggested links use Adamic-Adar: shared neighbours weighted by one over the log of their degree. In the tests PageRank, betweenness, clustering, assortativity and modularity agree with networkx to 1e-8 when it is installed.

docs.title: Geography
docs.text: Distances use the haversine formula on a sphere of radius 6371.0088 km (about 0.3 % off the true ellipsoid). Nearest-centre queries and neighbour searches use a ball tree on that metric. Zones come from DBSCAN with the haversine distance. Moran's I uses the k nearest neighbours of each point as binary links, row-standardised, and its p-value comes from shuffling the values (999 times by default); the expected value without a pattern is -1/(n-1). Getis-Ord Gi* sums each point and its neighbours, centres it on the global mean and divides by the standard deviation expected from the number of neighbours; the p-values of all points are corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg, so "hot spot" means significant after accounting for the number of places tested. Grid cells are cell_km tall and widened in longitude by the cosine of the mean latitude. A single projection of the sphere is used for all maps, so shapes far from the centre of a large area are distorted.

docs.title: Experiment checks
docs.text: The sample ratio test is a chi-square goodness-of-fit between the rows per group and the planned split; it alarms at p < 0.001 (the usual convention, because it is run on every test), and flags p between 0.001 and 0.05 as slightly off. Effects use Welch's t interval for numbers and a normal interval on the difference of proportions for 0/1 outcomes. CUPED replaces the outcome Y with Y - theta (X - mean(X)), where theta = cov(Y, X) / var(X) is estimated on all rows pooled so that it does not depend on the group; the variance falls by the squared correlation with X, which the page reports next to the observed narrowing of the interval, and a balance test on X flags assignment problems. Segments are compared with the rest of the rows through the difference of the two effects (a z test on the difference of differences), and the p-values of all segments are corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg. The smallest detectable effect is (z(0.975) + z(0.8)) * sqrt(2 sd^2 / n) for the smaller group, at 80 % power.

docs.title: Survey analysis
docs.text: Text answers are numbered from 1 when every non-empty answer belongs to one of the known scales (agreement, satisfaction, frequency, quality, and their Spanish versions). The favourable share counts the top two points and the unfavourable the bottom two. Cronbach's alpha is k/(k-1) (1 - sum of item variances / variance of the total) over the people who answered everything, with Feldt's F-based interval, and each question's correlation is with the sum of the others; on simulated items of known correlation it matches the theoretical value k r / (1 + (k - 1) r). The NPS interval uses the variance of promoters minus detractors, (p + d - (p - d)^2) / n. Groups are compared with the mix of detractors, passives and promoters through a chi-square test; the most extreme group is set aside and the rest tested again, so one outlier does not make every other group look different. Key drivers use Johnson's relative weights: with the correlation matrix of the questions R = P D P', L = P D^(1/2) P', beta = L^-1 r, and the weight of each question is (L squared) (beta squared), which adds up to the R squared of the regression and equals the squared correlation when questions are unrelated. Groups of questions are compared with Mann-Whitney (two) or Kruskal-Wallis (more), with rank-biserial correlation or epsilon squared as effect sizes, and Benjamini-Hochberg across questions.

docs.title: Concept lab
docs.text: Every concept is a seeded simulation (the same seed gives the same result) and is tested against its theory. The central limit theorem compares the spread of simulated averages with sigma over the square root of n; the p-value concept draws two groups from the same distribution, computes Student's t-test in vectorised form and, when looking several times, stops at the first significant look; the confidence-interval concept builds t intervals and measures coverage over 4,000 repetitions as well as over the 100 drawn; power uses the noncentral t distribution and checks one point by simulation; overfitting fits polynomials with a stable basis to repeated samples of sin(2 pi x) plus noise, and splits the error on fresh data into bias squared (distance of the average fit from the truth), variance (spread of the fits) and noise; Simpson's paradox generates groups whose x grows while their baseline y falls; regression to the mean makes each result skill plus luck with a chosen reliability, where the expected second result of the selected group is the reliability times the first; multiple testing runs the chosen number of tests per study and applies no correction, Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg. Parameters are checked against their allowed ranges before anything runs, so an absurd value gives a message instead of a long wait.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text: k-means on the standardized numeric columns, shown on the first two principal components. The inertia and silhouette chart helps pick k; the silhouette peak is a hint, not a rule.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: A recipe is a list of {operation, parameters} steps. The cleaning operations (fill missing, convert type, clip outliers, drop duplicates...) and the transformations share one registry, so any of them can be replayed. Applying a recipe to a new file runs the steps in order and stops at the first one that cannot apply, naming it. Operations that depend on the data itself (such as removing flagged anomalies) are not recorded. Joins refer to the extra dataset by name; supply it when replaying (-d name=path in the CLI).

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: A monitor stores its baseline as Parquet (after the recipe, if any), its settings and one JSON file per check. A check applies the recipe, reads dates and numbers stored as text, then compares against the baseline with the same machinery as Comparing datasets, scores with the model if one is set, and evaluates the rules. Alerts are high (drift at the high level, columns missing, a type change, a broken rule, an unreadable source), medium (a quality drop, which becomes high when it is twice the threshold; moderate drift when you asked for it; a change in rows; model inputs out of range, except missing columns, which are high; a prediction shift) or low (new columns). The status of a check is alert if any alert is high, warning if there are only lower ones, failed if the data could not be read and ok otherwise.

docs.title: Saved models
docs.text:
A model package holds the trained model together with:

  • the input schema: the original columns the model needs, their types, training ranges or categories, and share of empty values
  • the classes and the test metrics
  • for lab regressions, the 5th and 95th percentile of the test errors, which become the likely range of each prediction
  • optionally the recipe, so a raw file can be cleaned the same way before predicting

When scoring, the data are coerced to the training types (text like 1,200 becomes a number), missing columns are filled with empty values and reported, and the model's own imputation handles gaps. Predictions are only as trustworthy as the resemblance between the new data and the training data, which is what the warnings and the drift comparison measure.

Packages and .pkl files are Python pickles. Load only files you created yourself, because unpickling can run code.

docs.title: Python API and Jupyter
docs.text:
Everything the dashboard does is also available from Python, so you can use KikoLens inside a notebook (Jupyter, VS Code, Colab) or a script. Nothing leaves your machine.

import kikolens as kl

df = kl.load("sales.csv")        # a file, a link, a Google Sheet, a database...
kl.profile(df)                   # quality score, problems and a profile of every column
pilot = kl.autopilot(df)         # a first full analysis
lab = kl.lab(df, "revenue")      # compare models; lab.leaderboard, lab.pipeline, lab.metrics
lab.plot()                       # the main chart of any result

Run kikolens jupyter to get a quickstart notebook that builds its own sample data and walks through the calls below (it opens JupyterLab if it is installed: pip install "kikolens[jupyter]").

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every analysis returns a Result: a dictionary with attribute access that shows itself nicely in a notebook (a summary, notes and the main table) and keeps everything the analysis computed.

res = kl.forecast(df, "date", "revenue", horizon=14)
res.summary      # the sentence the dashboard shows
res.table        # the main table (here the forecast with its range)
res.plot()       # the main chart, a Plotly figure
res.best         # any other field: res.leaderboard, res.series ...

An unknown field raises an error that lists what is available. Text from your data is escaped in the notebook display.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Call What it does load(source, **kwargs) Read a dataset (the same sources as the dashboard). query(df, "select ... from df") Read-only SQL; the table is called df. Returns a DataFrame. ask(df, "question") A local model (Ollama) writes the SQL and it is run. profile(df) Quality score, problems and column profile. dictionary(df, descriptions=None) A data dictionary: one row per column. scan_privacy(df) Columns that look like personal data. autopilot(df, target=None) Clean, find patterns, model a column and forecast dates. lab(df, target, **kwargs) The model lab; keyword arguments as in the lab (models, folds, tune, drop, ...). forecast(df, date, value, horizon=12, agg="mean") Five models tested on the past; the best one forecasts. anomalies(df, **kwargs) Unusual rows and why. spikes(df, date, value) Unusual periods once trend and season are removed. drift(reference, current) Which columns changed between two datasets. why(df, metric, date, **kwargs) Why a figure changed between two periods. regress(df, target, features=None) Linear (number) or logistic (two values) regression, explained. survival(df, duration, event, group=None) Kaplan-Meier curves and a log-rank test. cohorts(df, user, date) / rfm(df, customer, date, amount) Retention and customer segments. distribution(series) Which distribution fits a column best. chart(df, "request") A chart described in words (needs Ollama): res.figure, res.table, res.spec. analyst(df) A conversation: bot = kl.analyst(df); bot.ask("why did revenue fall?") returns a turn with .text, .figure, .table, .sql and the steps taken in .report. classify_text(texts, ["a", "b"]) Zero-shot classification of texts with the local model. formula(df, "revenue per unit") A formula for a new column described in words, already checked with the safe interpreter (name, expression, preview). link(left, right, left_on, right_on) Fuzzy match by names; res.merged has the joined table. select_features(df, target) Which columns to keep: consensus of four methods and a cross-validated curve; res.recommended, res.removable. segment(df, "gmm" \| "hierarchical" \| "dbscan") Segments with each group described in words; res.labels is the group of every row. ab_sequential(df, group, outcome, control, order=None) A sequential A/B test that stays valid when checked after every observation. granger(df, date, cause, effect) / forecast_drivers(df, date, target, drivers, scenario=...) Granger test; forecast using other columns, with what-if scenarios. effect(df, treatment, outcome, covariates=None, method="aipw") Causal effect with five estimators side by side; res.effect, res.interval, res.table, res.balance, res.e_value. uplift(df, treatment, outcome, covariates=None) Effect per row and who to target; res.cate, res.deciles, res.qini. discontinuity(df, running, outcome, cutoff) Effect of crossing a threshold, with a bandwidth sweep. synthetic_control(df, unit, time, outcome, treated_unit, intervention) Effect on one unit against a synthetic control; res.p_value comes from placebos. instrumental(df, outcome, endogenous, instruments, covariates=None) Two-stage least squares; res.first_stage_f tells whether the instrument is strong. likert(df, items) / cronbach(df, items) / nps(df, score, group=None) / crosstab(df, row, column) Survey basics: scale summary, reliability, Net Promoter Score, cross-tab with residuals. key_drivers(df, outcome, items) / compare_items(df, items, group) / response_quality(df, items) What matters most for an overall rating (res.table with importance and priority); questions that differ between groups; answer-quality flags. concepts() / concept(name, seed=0, **params) The concept lab: a table of simulations, and one run with res.summary, res.lesson, res.figure and its numbers. glossary(term=None, lang="en") The glossary: a table of all terms, the definition of one ("p_value" or "p-value"), or the terms that match a word. panel(df, path=None, definition=None, where=None) A panel of metrics, charts and tables. With a path ending in .html it writes the file; without one it returns the Panel to add tiles to. stationarity(df, date, value) / autocorrelation(df, date, value) ADF and KPSS with suggested differences; autocorrelation with Ljung-Box. governance() / governance("promote", "model", to="production") The governance overview, or one action (register, update, validate, approve, checks, promote, rollback). model_card("model") returns the card as Markdown. topics(df, text, k=None, date=None) Topics (res.table, res.assignments, res.coherence; with date, res.over_time). near_duplicates(df, text), similar(df, text, "a phrase"), text_patterns(df, text), keyphrases(df, text) and readability(df, text) work on one text column. network(df, source, target, weight=None, directed=False) Network analysis from a list of links: res.table (PageRank, betweenness, clustering, community per node), res.communities, res.modularity. network_path, suggest_links and network_robustness take the same columns. geo_check(df) / geo_distances(df, centers) / geo_hotspots(df) / spatial_autocorrelation(df, value) / geo_grid(df) Geography on a table with latitude and longitude columns, found by name (or give lat= and lon=). centers is a (lat, lon) pair or a table with center_lat=, center_lon=, center_name=. experiment(df, group, outcome, control, pre=None, date=None, segments=None) Full A/B analysis; res.verdict, res.table, res.srm, and with the options res.cuped, res.over_time, res.segments. srm(df, group) and cuped(df, group, outcome, pre, control) run one step. decompose_stl(df, date, value, period=None) Robust STL; res.components, res.seasonal_strength, res.trend_strength. arima(df, date, value, order=None, seasonal=(0,0,0), period=None, horizon=12) Seasonal ARIMA; without order it searches (res.candidates). res.forecast, res.backtest, res.ljung_box. recommender(df, user, item, rating=None) An item-based recommender: .recommend(person), .similar_items(item), .popular(). synthesize(df, n=None) Synthetic data; res.data is the table and res.report the fidelity and privacy figures. runs(target=None) The history of model lab runs (the dashboard and kikolens lab record them). save_model(lab_result, df, name) / score(df, "name") Keep a model and predict with it later. Only open model files you trust.

docs.title: Magics
docs.text:
%load_ext kikolens
%kl_profile df            # quality of a DataFrame
%kl_autopilot df revenue  # a first analysis, predicting 'revenue'
%kl_privacy df            # columns that look like personal data

%%kl_sql df
select region, sum(revenue) as revenue from df group by region

The cell magic takes the name of a DataFrame and runs the body as a read-only query.

docs.title: Reproduce a session
docs.text: The dashboard's Export → Notebook tab and kikolens notebook data.csv analysis.ipynb --recipe recipe.json --target revenue write a notebook that reloads the data, repeats every recipe step and trains a model.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text: Six end-to-end paths that use the sample files in examples/. Each can be done in the dashboard or from the terminal.

docs.title: 1. From a messy file to a model you can reuse
docs.text:
Goal: clean sales_demo.csv, find a good model for revenue, and keep it.

Dashboard Terminal Quality and cleaning: press Auto-clean (trims text, drops the 7 duplicate rows, turns date into dates and unit_price from text into numbers). kikolens clean examples/sales_demo.csv --output clean.csv --save-recipe recipe.json Model lab: choose revenue, leave out units, run it. Read the leaderboard, then the diagnostics. kikolens lab clean.csv revenue --exclude units --register sales-model Predict: Save to my models. (already saved by --register)

Why leave out units? In this synthetic data it is almost a copy of revenue, so a model that includes it just reads the answer off that column and looks excellent (R² around 0.9 from one column). Leaving it out forces the model to learn from the date, region, channel, price and discount, which is the question that matters if you want to predict revenue before the units are known. The lab's leakage check looks for columns that are nearly perfect copies of the target; a column like units that is highly informative but not identical is for you to judge.

When a CSV is read, dates and numbers written as text (2023-01-01, 1,200) are recognized and used as dates and numbers when modeling; the lab tells you which columns it read that way. The recipe and the model package keep the cleaning steps and the columns the model expects, so you do not need to remember either.

docs.title: 2. Score a new quarter
docs.text:
Goal: apply the same cleaning to sales_new_quarter.csv, predict its revenue, and check whether the model can still be trusted.

kikolens apply examples/sales_new_quarter.csv recipe.json --output new_clean.csv
kikolens score new_clean.csv sales-model --output predictions.csv
kikolens drift clean.csv new_clean.csv --output drift.csv

In the dashboard: Predict with Predict a file and the Another file option (tick Apply the cleaning steps used for training first to skip the first command), then Compare data with Another file against the open one.

What you will see:

  • score warns that the dates are later than anything in training and that many unit_price values are above the training range.
  • drift reports channel, region and unit_price as drifted (more online sales, a bigger West share, higher prices), and revenue as well because it trends upward. It exits with code 2.
  • The predictions still run, but they are less accurate: in our run the average error on the new quarter was about twice the error on the held-out test, and only a little over half of the actual values fell inside the predicted range that should hold about 90% of the time. That gap is exactly what the warnings and the drift report are telling you. Retrain with recent data before relying on them.

docs.title: 3. Understand what drives a result
docs.text:
Goal: find out which factors are really associated with revenue, without fooling yourself.

  1. Experiments → What relates to... → target revenue (terminal: kikolens screen clean.csv revenue). All columns are tested together and corrected for chance. In the sample data only units is related (rank correlation 0.95); unit_price, region and discount are not, even though each would have looked "interesting" in a chart.
  2. Experiments → Compare groups: revenue by region. The ANOVA gives p ≈ 0.27 and an effect size of 0.01 ("negligible"): the regional averages differ only as much as chance would produce with this many rows, and the page says that this does not prove there is no difference.
  3. Dimensions → Redundant columns: revenue and units both get a VIF around 10.8 ("severe"), meaning each is mostly explained by the other. Do not read one as an explanation of the other.
  4. Model lab → Explain: permutation importance and the partial dependence of the top feature, for the model with units left out.

docs.title: 4. Enrich, test and ship
docs.text:
Goal: join manager targets to the sales, compare channels with an A/B test, and share the result.

  1. Transform → Combine: upload regions.csv, join on region (left). Each row now carries its manager and target.
  2. Transform → Columns → Formula: share_of_target = revenue / target.
  3. Experiments → A/B test: group channel, control Store, outcome revenue (terminal: kikolens ab clean.csv channel revenue --control Store). In the sample data Online averages 1,888 against 1,881 for Store (+0.4%, 95% interval −41 to +55, p ≈ 0.78): no reliable difference. The page also tells you that detecting a gap this small would take on the order of 24,000 rows per group, which is the honest answer to "should we invest in this channel because of this data?".
  4. Anomalies: review the 2% most unusual days (kikolens anomalies clean.csv --share 2); each comes with the reason it was flagged. Remove them only if they are errors, not real events.
  5. Project → Save: write your notes, tick Include trained models and download the .kikolens file. Report builds the HTML page for others.

The steps in 1 and 2 are recorded in the recipe; the join needs regions.csv supplied again when you replay it (kikolens apply data.csv recipe.json --output out.csv -d examples/regions.csv).

docs.title: 5. Watch a data feed
docs.text:
Goal: be told when a data source that keeps being updated stops looking like the data a model was trained on.

kikolens clean examples/sales_demo.csv --output clean.csv --save-recipe recipe.json
kikolens lab clean.csv revenue --exclude units --register sales-model
kikolens validate clean.csv --save rules.json                       # rules suggested by the data
kikolens monitor create sales-feed clean.csv --model sales-model --recipe recipe.json --rules rules.json
kikolens monitor run sales-feed                                     # the baseline against itself: OK, exit code 0
kikolens monitor run sales-feed --source examples/sales_new_quarter.csv

The last command prints ALERT and exits with code 2. Its alerts: drift (5 of 6 columns), the drop from 540 rows to 120, the dates and prices outside what the model saw, and the average prediction up by 22%. The rules still pass: nothing in the new quarter is invalid, it is just different. In the dashboard, Models → Monitoring shows the same history as a chart and a table; Schedule it prints the commands to run the check every day or every hour, and kikolens monitor watch sales-feed keeps running and checks whenever the file changes. Add --webhook https://... if you want a short message posted when a check ends in an alert.

docs.title: 6. Read customer comments
docs.text:
Goal: find out what people complain about in reviews.csv and what goes with a low rating.

  1. Analysis → Text → Terms: the commonest words (kikolens text examples/reviews.csv review). Search a word, such as courier, to read it in context.
  2. By group, Terms that go with a higher or lower number, choosing rating: comments that mention courier or tracking average about 2 stars against about 3.6 for the rest, while great and battery average about 4.7. That is the shipping problem and the product strength, without anyone having tagged them.
  3. Themes with 3 groups gives the topics the comments fall into, each with its key terms and an example.
  4. Classify, predicting rating: it reaches about 44% against 30% for always guessing the commonest rating, which is a modest gain; the page tells you when a classifier is no better than guessing. Ratings are noisy (one star either way), so the text carries only part of the signal.
  5. Summary (needs Ollama) asks the local model for the main themes and complaints of a sample.

docs.title: 7. Start from a file you have never seen
docs.text:
Goal: know what is in a new file in two minutes.

kikolens autopilot examples/sales_demo.csv --clean clean.csv --recipe recipe.json --pdf summary.pdf

It cleans, guesses that revenue is the column to predict, compares four models against a baseline, forecasts the series and writes a PDF. In the dashboard, Data → Autopilot does the same and one button applies its cleaning to your data. From there, the Model lab is the careful version.

docs.title: 8. Retention and a campaign
docs.text:
Goal: see whether customers come back, who is worth keeping, and whether a campaign worked.

  1. Analysis → Customers → Retention with your customer and date columns: the share of each monthly cohort still active later.
  2. Segments (RFM) shows the segments that hold most of the value and who is at risk of leaving.
  3. Analysis → Impact → Before and after a date: pick the metric and the campaign date. Add control series, such as a region the campaign did not reach, to make the estimate much sturdier. The range comes from how wrong the method was on earlier periods.

From the terminal: kikolens cohorts orders.csv user date, kikolens rfm orders.csv user date amount --output segments.csv and kikolens impact daily.csv date sales --at 2024-06-01 --control visits.

docs.title: 9. Why did revenue drop?
docs.text:
Goal: find which part of the business moved a figure.

  1. Analysis → Why it changed, measure a total of revenue, with the date column. The two periods start as the last third of the dates against the one before.
  2. The ranking tells you which column concentrates the change; the waterfall shows each value's contribution, and the combinations table names the regions and channels that moved most together.

From the terminal: kikolens why sales.csv date --metric revenue --before 2024-03-01,2024-05-01 --after 2024-05-01,2024-07-01.

docs.title: 10. Put a model behind a small API
docs.text:
kikolens lab clean.csv revenue --register sales-model
kikolens serve sales-model --port 8000
curl -X POST localhost:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"rows": [{"date": "2023-06-01", "region": "North", "channel": "Online", "units": 120, "unit_price": 3200, "discount": 0.1}]}'

The reply has the predictions (with a range for regression) and warnings about missing columns, unseen categories or out-of-range values. The server listens only on this computer; to open it to the network use --host 0.0.0.0 --token SECRET and send Authorization: Bearer SECRET. Only serve model files you trust, because opening one can run code.

docs.title: 11. Share data safely
docs.text:
Goal: hand a dataset to someone else without exposing people.

  1. Data → Privacy (or kikolens privacy customers.csv --scan) lists the columns that hold personal data and why they were flagged.
  2. Choose for each: hash the customer email (it stays usable to count and join), mask the card number, remove the full name. The steps join the recipe.
  3. The How identifiable tab (--k 5 --quasi age,city) shows whether age, postal code and city together still single someone out. If many rows are alone in their group, group the ages into bands (Transform → bins) or drop a column, and check again.
  4. Export → Data dictionary documents what each column means for the person receiving it.
kikolens privacy customers.csv --hash email --mask card --drop full_name --salt "$SALT" --output shared.csv --recipe privacy.json
kikolens privacy shared.csv --k 5 --quasi age,city

Keep privacy.json private: it contains the salt.

docs.title: 12. Run the same analysis every morning
docs.text:
Put the steps in a pipeline file and let a scheduler run it (see Pipeline files in the command reference):

kikolens run pipeline.json || echo "Something changed: look at out/log.json"

docs.title: 13. Stop an A/B test as soon as you can
docs.text:
Goal: know whether a variant wins without waiting for a fixed number of visitors, and without fooling yourself by peeking.

  1. Analysis → Sequential tests → Planner: with a 10% conversion rate and a change of 2 points, compare the fixed-size test with the sequential one and see that false alarms stay near 5% even when checked after every visitor.
  2. Export the visits in order (one row per visitor, the variant and a 0/1 for conversion) and open Live test: the evidence line shows when it crosses the threshold, and the always-valid p-value and range say how much to trust the difference.
  3. Not sure the variants are equal? The Bandit simulator shows how much traffic would have gone to the winner while learning.

From the terminal: kikolens ab-seq visits.csv variant converted control --order timestamp.

docs.title: 14. What should I keep for the model?
docs.text:
1. Models → Feature selection on your target. Four methods vote; the curve shows that a handful of columns is as good as all of them.
  2. Remove the columns I can leave out adds a recipe step, so the same cut is applied to new data.
  3. Train with the Model lab using Bayesian tuning, and look at Run history to see that the new run beats the previous ones.

docs.title: 15. Share data you cannot share
docs.text: Privacy removes or fingerprints the identifying columns; Synthetic data then generates a table with the same distributions and correlations whose rows are not people. Its report shows the fidelity, the exact and near copies of real rows, and how well a model trained on it does on real rows. kikolens synth customers.csv shareable.csv --report.

docs.title: 16. Talk to your data
docs.text:
Goal: get answers without knowing which section to open. Needs Ollama and a model (ollama pull llama3.2).

  1. Data → Analyst, with the sales example loaded: "show the total revenue by region" draws a bar chart, and the How the chart was built expander shows the specification the model wrote.
  2. "How many rows per channel?" runs a SQL query and shows it.
  3. "What drives revenue?" hands over to the agent; open Steps taken to see each tool it chose and why, and download the trail as Python to repeat it without the model.

From the terminal: kikolens analyst sales.csv "why did revenue change?" --trail steps.py, kikolens chart sales.csv "average revenue by month" --output chart.html, kikolens classify-text reviews.csv review --labels shipping,quality,price.

docs.title: Monitoring from a script or CI
docs.text:
kikolens drift returns exit code 2 when the data changed a lot, 0 otherwise. A nightly job can compare the latest export with the data the model was trained on:

kikolens drift training.csv latest.csv || echo "Data changed: review before trusting predictions"
kikolens validate latest.csv rules.json || echo "Rules broken"
kikolens monitor run sales-feed || echo "See kikolens monitor history sales-feed"
